full_judgment:
Md Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: This appeal is directed at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant against the judgment and decree dated 24-10-2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka allowing an application so field by the present respondent Nos. 1-7 as defendants under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure through which the learned judge rejected the plaint.
2. The short facts leading to preferring this appeal are:
The present appellant as plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit with the following prayers:
অতএব, উপরোক্ত কারণাধীনে ন্যায় বিচারের স্বার্থে বাদীর বিনীত প্রার্থনা এই যে,
(ক) নিম্ন নালিশী তফসিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তি বাদীর ১ ঘোষণা মালিক উত্তরাধিকার মর্মে এক স্বত্ব ঘোষণার ডিক্রী দিতেঃ
(খ) নালিশী নিন্ন তফসিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তি ঢাকা সিটি জরিপের ৪৩ নং খতিয়ানের ১৪ নং খতিয়ানে ১৪৫৮৬ পল্লবী দাগ যাহা মিরপুর হালে পল্পবী থানার সেনপাড়া পর্বতা মৌজার ১৮৬৮ শতাংশ সম্পত্তি কাতে ৯ শতাংশ সম্পত্তি ১নং বিবাদীর নামে রেকর্ড হওয়া ভুল, ভ্রমাত্মক, তঞ্চরুতা, শঠতা বেআইনী বাদী কিংবা তাহার স্থলাবর্তী ওয়ারিশগনের উপর বাধ্যকর ও কার্যকর নয় মর্মে এক ঘোষণার ডিক্রি দিতেঃ
(গ) আদালতের সম্যক ব্যয় বাদীর পক্ষে এবং বিবাদীদের প্রতিকূলে ডিক্রী দিতে
(ঘ) আইন ও ইকুইটি মতে বাদী আরো যে সকল প্রতিকার পাইতে হকদার সে সকল আদেশ দিতে মর্জি হয়।
3. Soon after filing of the suit, the present respondent Nos. 1-7 as defendant Nos. 1-7 filed an application under clause (a) and (d) of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of plaint contending inter alia that, there has been no cause of action in the suit and the suit land is unspecified. Though against the said application for rejection of plaint filed by the defendants, no written objection was filed by the present plaintiff-appellant. It is mentionable that, after filing of the suit the plaintiff also filed an application for temporary injunction restraining the respondent. Nos. 1-7 from dispossessing them from the suit land against which the present opposite parties filed written objection. Anyway, the application for rejection of plaint was taken up for hearing by the learned Joint District Judge and vide impugned order dated 24-10-2018 allowed the application and thereby rejected the plaint chiefly holding that, the plaint is not specified (মোকদ্দমার আরজী সুনির্দিষ্ট না হওয়ায় আিইনানুগভাবে উহা রক্ষণীয় নয়)and arrived at a finding that the suit is not maintainable.
4. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said order rejecting the plaint, the plaintiff as appellant preferred this appeal.
5. Mr Iqbal Kalam Chowdhury, the learned counsel appearing for the appellant upon taking us to the impugned order and those of the plaint, application filed under Order VII, rule 11 so annexed with the application for injunction at the very outset submits that, though it is on the record that, the defendants filed the said application relying clause (a) and (d) but on that very legal point, there has been no discussion in the impugned order rather the learned judge invited some extraneous facts , which does not attract the provision provided in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
6. The learned counsel for the appellant upon taking us to the application for rejection of plaint in particular, paragraph No. 7 to the plaint then contends that, there has been specific date described therein about arising cause of action for filing the suit yet the learned judge in a very perfunctory manner rejected the plaint without considering so.
7. The learned counsel by taking us to paragraph No. 14 to 'the application for rejection of plaint also contends that, even in that paragraph the defendants refuted the cause of action whereby it clearly proves of existing a cause of action but whether that very cause of action is correct or not it will only be decided at trial upon taking evidence of the parties concerned.
8. The learned counsel goes on to contend that, though the application was filed basing on clause (d) of Order VII, rule 11 but in the four corners of the application filed for rejection of plaint let alone in the impugned order there has been any discussion to that effect.
9. The learned counsel wrapped up his submission submitting that, the learned judge has rejected the plaint just observing that, the boundary so described in the schedule of the plaint does not match with the boundary provided in the application for rejection of plaint and basing on that assertion, the plaint was rejected which cannot be any point in rejecting a plaint within the meaning of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and finally prays for allowing the appeal.
10. On the contrary, Mr AKM Zakir Uzzaman Khan, the learned counsel appearing for the defendant-respondent Nos. 2-7 by taking us to the application for rejection of plaint at the very outset submits that, since the suit land as well as averment made in the plaint over the claim is totally different so the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree in the form of declaration of title.
11. The learned counsel by referring to the application for rejection of plaint in particular, paragraph No. 8 thereof also contends that, the boundary (চৌহদ্দি) described in the last portion of the plaint is totally different from what has described in that very paragraph and the licarried judge has rightly rejected the plaint which warrants no interference by this Hon'ble court.
12. When we pose a question to the learned counsel for the respondents whether the learned judge has taken into consideration either clause (a) or clause (d) of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the learned counsel then finds it difficult to reply the said query as admittedly there has been no discussion on those legal ingredients in the impugned order and finally prays for dismissing the appeal.
<u>13. We have considered the submission so placed by the learned counsel for the appellant and that of the respondent Nos. 2-7 at length. We have also gone through the provision laid down in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that of the application filed by the present opposite parties under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The said application is found to be very specific because in that application the defendants have mentioned two specific clause that is, clause (a) and (d), clause (a) speaks for cause of action when clause (d) refers to barring any suit under law. But on going through the plaint, we clearly find there describes cause of action in filing the suit and defendants refuted that cause of action in their application for rejection of plaint so under no circumstances, can it be found that there has been no cause of action in the suit. Secondly, though the defendants-respondents also based on clause (d) but the suit was filed for declaration of title simpliciter under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Since the suit was filed challenging the propriety of latest record prepared in the name of the defendants so suit is amply entertainable in its present form having no occasion to find the suit is barred by any law. 14. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances, we don't find any iota of substance in the impugned order which is liable to be set-aside.</u>
15. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. 16. The impugned order dated 24-10-2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 732 of 2016 is thus set-aside.
17. The learned Joint District Judge, 2nd court, Dhaka is hereby directed to proceed with the Title Suit No. 732 of 2016 as expeditiously as possible. Let a copy of this order be communicated to the said learned judge forthwith.
End.

full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, C. J: This civil appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 19.08.2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.185 of 2010 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and order dated 09.11.2009 passed by the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 230 of 2009 dismissing the same affirming those dated 20.07.2009 passed by Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No.27 of 2009 dismissing the application under order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
2. The relevant facts, for the disposal of this appeal, are that on 26.04.2003 the appellant Sonali Bank Limited, filed Artha Rin Suit No.131 of 2003 against respondent No.4 and another for realization of Tk.47,40,875/- stating that one Saleha Khatun (now dead) and her son Abdul Latif, took loan by mortgaging the scheduled land including the structures thereon. Said suit was decreed ex-parte. Execution Case No.355 of 2004 was started on 01.06.2004 and the Adalat invited tender notice for selling the scheduled land in auction which was published in “The Daily Prothom Alo” and “ The Dainik Sangbad” on 13.08.2005, but no one participated in auction. Then, the decreeholder bank made a prayer before the Adalat on 08.01.2006 to issue certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Accordingly, certificate was issued on 09.01.2007. On the basis of the said certificate, the decree holder bank invited tender notice for holding auction of the scheduled property. The tender notice was published in “The Daily Janakantha” on 23.04.2009. Following the invitation of tender notice, the scheduled property was sold in auction and, accordingly, a deed was registered on 29.06.2009 in favour of the auction purchaser. Thereafter, the respondent No.1 along with three others filed an application on 04.05.2009 under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Adalat for getting release of the scheduled property, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No.27 of 2009. They also submitted a bond amounting to 10% of the decretal dues. The decree holder bank contested the said Miscellaneous case which was, ultimately, dismissed on 20.07.2009. Then the respondent No.1 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.230 of 2009 which was dismissed on 09.11.2009. Thereafter, the respondent No.1, filing revisional application in the High Court Division, obtained Rule. The High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 19.08.2010 made the Rule absolute. Thus, the Sonali Bank Limited has preferred this appeal upon getting leave.
3. Mr. A.M. Amin Uddin, learned Senior Counsel, with Mr. Biswajit Debnath, Deputy Attorney General (instructed by Ms. Mahmuda Begum, Advocate-on-Record) appearing for the appellant, submits that the Execution Case was finally disposed of under section 33(9) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 on 22.02.2007 and, thereafter, the application under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the respondent No.1. So, there was no scope of entertaining such application. The High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute. He further submits that the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that application filed by the respondent No.1 under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable after sale of the mortgaged property, particularly, in a proceeding under Artha Rin Adalat Ain. He, lastly, submits that respondent No.1 Most. Salma Begom is one of the heirs of the judgment debtor late Saleha Khatun. Therefore, her application under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not sustainable, the High Court Division erred in entertaining such application.
4. Mr. A.F. Hassan Ariff, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent No.1, in his submission, supported the judgment and order of the High Court Division.
5. The plaintiff bank filed instant Artha Suit against the respondent No.1 and all the heirs and successors of late Jummun Miah for realization of outstanding loan amount of Tk.42,85,027/- and interest till realization of outstanding dues and got decree. Thereafter, decree holder bank filed Execution Case. In order to realize the total dues, the bank obtained certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 on 09.01.2007 which authorises the Adalat to issue certificate vesting the right of possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged property and authority to transfer/ sell the mortgaged property. Thereafter, the decree holder bank published a tender notice in “the daily Janokantho” and sold the scheduled property in auction on 29.06.2009.
<u>6. It appears from the materials on record that earlier Salma Begum filed Writ Petition No.7932 of 2009 against impugned order of the Adalat, which was rejected summarily on 24.11.2009. They filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 199 of 2009 in this Division which was also dismissed. This Court earlier refused to entertain such prayer of the respondent No.1 treating her prayer as an application under section 32 of the Ain. Now, she has adopted the instant procedure claiming her prayer as an application under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Under the aforesaid provision, an application has to be filed where any claim is preferred to, or any objection is made to the attachment of, any property attached in execution of a decree on the ground that such property is not liable to such attachment, the Court, shall proceed to investigate the claim or objection with the like power as regards the examination of the claimant objector, and in all respects, as if he was a party to the suit. Rule 59 provides that claimant or objector must adduce evidence to show that at the date of the attachment he had some interest in or was possessed of, the property attached. The aforesaid provisions contemplated an inquiry into questions including questions relating to right, title or interest in the property attached. It seems to us, having regard to the relevant provisions, that the stage at which a claim is to be preferred under Order XXI Rule 58 is intended to be a stage before the sale has actually been held and the attachment is pending. It is open to the Court under sub-rule(2), Rule 58 to postpone the sale pending investigation of the claim. In the instant case auction has already been held at the instance of the bank itself after getting certificate under section 33(5) of the Ain. The High Court Division acted in excess of its authority in allowing claim petition preferred under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure after the property attached was sold. A reading of the provisions indicates that it can be by a person other than the party to the suit. Moreover, earlier this Division and the High Court Division have maintained the impugned order of the Adalat.</u>
7. Accordingly, we find merit in the instant appeal.
8. Thus, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order dated 19.08.2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 185 of 2010 is hereby set aside.
End.

full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman J.: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 15.03.2010 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.841 of 1999 making the Rule absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree dated 04.01.1999 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong in Other Appeal No.122 of 1997 reversing those dated 27.02.1997 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 2nd Additional Court at Sadar, Chittagong in Other Suit No.61 of 1990. 

2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the respondent No.1 as plaintiff instituted suit for specific performance of contract against the defendant-petitioner and others stating, inter alia, that the defendant No.1 proposed to sell the suit land and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same at consideration of Tk.10,000/-. The defendant No.1 receiving Tk.6020/- as earnest money, executed a "bainanama" on 30.07.1975 in favour of the plaintiff and handed over possession of the suit land. The plaintiff, thereafter, offered the balance consideration and demanded execution and registration of the sale deed from the defendant No.1 but he tend to avoid making some pretexts. The plaintiff issued legal notice on 29.12.1975 to the defendant demanding execution and registration of the said deed but the defendant No.1 did not execute the deed. Hence the suit. 

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 3-4 contested the suit by filling two separate sets of writ-ten statements denying the materials allegations made in the plaint. The defendant No.1 contended that he did not make any agreement to sale the suit land to the plaintiff. He is in possession of the same through his monthly tenants. 

4. The defendant Nos.3 and 4 contended that the defendant No.1 proposed to sell the suit land, made an agreement with these defendants on 02.12.1974 receiving Tk.10,000/- out of total consideration of Tk.25,000/- and delivered possession. The defendant No.1 denied to execute and register the sale deed. Accordingly, these defendants filed Title Suit No.23 of 1977 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong and got a compromise decree. These defendants had no knowledge about the "bainanama" of the plaintiff. 

5. The plaintiff by amending the plaint sought for declaration that the kabala deed executed by the defendant No. 1 in favour of the defendant Nos.3-4 pursuant to the decree passed in Other Suit No.23 of 1977, are void, collusive, ineffective and the same is not binding upon the plaintiff. He further prayed for declaration that the decree obtained by the defendant Nos.3 and 4 in Other Class Suit No.23 of 1977 is also void and the same is not binding upon the plaintiff. 

6. On conclusion of the trial, the learned Assistant Judge, 2nd Additional Court at Sadar, Chittagong considering the evidences and documents on record decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 27.02.1997. 

7. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant Nos.3-4 as appellant preferred Other Appeal No.122 of 1997 before the learned District Judge, Chittagong. On transfer, the said appeal was heard by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 3rd Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong who by his judgment and decree dated 04.01.1999 allowed the appeal and there-by set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

8. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree dated 04.01.1999 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 3rd Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong, the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No.841 of 1999 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule. 

9. In due course, a Single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the par-ties made the Rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 15.03.2010 and thereby set aside the judgment and decree dated 04.01.1999 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 3rd Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong in Title Appeal No.122 of 1997 and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree dated 27.02.1997 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 2nd Additional Court at Sadar, Chittagong in Other Suit No.61 of 1990. 

10. The defendant Nos.3 and 4 as petitioners herein feeling aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 15.03.2010 of the High Court Division preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1114 of 2010 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal. 

11. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that having regard to the admitted fact that the land described in the "bainanama" of the plaintiff and that of the decree these defendant appellants are not the same lands and having further regard to the fact that the High Court Division came to the finding that the suit land of Other Suit No. 61 of 1990/54 of 1976  are not identical with the suit land in Other Suit No.23 of 1977 and there is no clash of interest between the defendant Nos.3-4 and the plaintiff with respect to the agreement as Ext.4-bainanama, but the High Court Division committed an error of law in set-ting aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court. He further submits that the High Court Division has committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiff, by filing Other Suit No. 61 of 1990/54 of 1976 for specific performance of contract, has not acquired any legal right in the suit land and hence, he is not entitled to get declaration that the judgment and decree passed in another suit between different parties being Other Suit No.23 of 1977 in respect of the different suit land as illegal and void and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. However, he finally concedes that he has no submission against the decree of the suit land so far it relates to a decree of specific performance of contract. 

12. Per contra, Mr. Mostafa Newaz Mohammad, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent No.1 made submissions in supports of the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. He submits that the plaintiff proved the fact of a valid contract, due execution of agreement by Shishu Bala and payment of earnest money and the suit was instituted within time, and the defendants failed to discard or contradict those facts. Hence, the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute and legally restored the judgment and decree of the trial Court by setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below. Therefore, he prays for dismissal of the appeal. However, after submissions of the learned Senior Counsel Mr. Alam regarding no objection about the decree for specific performance of contract in favour of the plaintiff. Mr. Mostafa Neaz Mohammad very candidly submits that he has no objection if the judgment is modified to that effect as per submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants. 

13. We have heard the learned Senior Counsels for the respective parties. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

14. Leave was granted to examine the submissions of the learned Senior Advocate for the appellants as to that having regard to the admitted fact that the land described in the "Bainanama" of the plaintiff and that of the decree these are not the same lands and having further regard to the fact that the High Court Division came to the finding that the suit land of Other Suit No. 61 of 1990 are not identical with the Other suit no. 54 of 1976 and there is no clash of interest between the defendant nos. 3-4 and the plaintiff with respect to the agreement Exhibit no. 4 (Bainanama). That the Single Judge committed an error of law in setting aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate court. That the High Court Division has committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiff, by filing Other Suit No. 54 of 1976 (Other Suit No. 61 of 1990) for specific performance of contract, has not acquired any legal right in the suit land as such he is not entitled to get declaration that the judgment and decree passed in another suit between different parties being Other Suit No. 23 of 1977 in respect of the different suit land as illegal and void. 

15. At this moment let us weigh up the evidence on record, state of affairs of the cases, and decisions of the three (03) Courts below, whether judgment and order of High Court Division is justified or erred which calls for interference by this Division.  
16. For obtaining a decree meant for specific performance of contract the plaintiff is required to prove the existence of a valid contract, execution of an agreement fairly and without any inducement, coercion or fraud and the question of limitation. 

17. In the instant case the plaintiffs of the Other Suit No. 61 of 1990 has been able to prove clue execution of the agreement and payment of earnest money by adducing witnesses to the agreement and that was not discarded or successfully contradicted during cross-examination. The Defendant no. 1 Shishu Bala Barua, even though submitted written statement, however, did not contest the suit. The present suit being Other Suit No. 61 of 1976 was instituted on 06.04.1976 and the agreement was executed on 30.07.1975 which means, the suit was instituted within prescribed limitation period. 

18. In view of the above the discussions the decision of the Appellant Court in dismissing the suit as a whole is found to be based upon total non application of judicial mind and not been supported by evidence. As such, it should be reversed and the judgment and order of the trial court as far as the judgments and decrees relate the relief of specific performance of contract. 

19. On careful perusal of the schedules of the impugned Bainanama (exhibit no. 4) of the Other suit no. 61 of 1990 and Kabala nos. 7321 and 7322 of 1977 (exhibit no. Kha and Kha-1) of the other suit no. 23 of 1977 it was found that suit lands of the two cases are not identical. High Court Division too opine in the same line in its impugned judgment and order. Even so, High Court Division affirmed the trial court's decision declaring the registered Kabala nos. 7321 and 7322 of 1977 as void, illegal, without consideration in pursuance of its order of cancellation of judgment and decree of the other suit no. 23 of 1977. Consequently, our considered view is that High Court Division erred in law as well as fact on the face of the record resulting failure of justice in affirming the trial court's decision in toto. 

20. Moreover, trial court reached in the decision of declaring the aforementioned two Kabalas as void, illegal, without consideration etc on the grounds and reasoning that the Kabalas were executed and registered on the same day of the compromise decree, as such, these were fraudulently executed and registered. However, without solid concrete basis it is not legally sustainable. The mere fact that the execution and registration of the Kabalas were taken at the same date can no way be deem as an, ingredient of conspiracy and swindle. In this context this Division's observations made in the case of Capital Tower Limited vs. Mirpur Mazar Co-operative Market Society Ltd. and others reported in 2005 25 BLD (AD) 91 that: 
"The facts and circumstances upon noting which the High Court Division held the lease in question as collusive and fraudulent in our view in the background of the facts and circumstances noticed by us, is not legally sustainable. The mere fact that decision on the application for allotment of the land and the registration of the lease deed were taken at a short span of time can no way be considered as an, element of collusion and fraud since it is seen from the materials on record that the plot allotted to the defendant No. 6 has been made upon observing the procedure relating to the allotment of the land followed by the Respondent Nos. 1-5 and the land has been allotted upon pricing the same correctly." 

21. On the other hand, we cannot approve too the appellate courts observations that as a court of lower grade the learned Assistant Judge cannot cancel the judgment and decree of 02 grade senior court of a Joint District Judge. Trial court based its decision of cancellation of judgment and decree on findings of fraudulent practices and 'collusions. Because, it is an established rule of administration of justice that fraud vitiates everything. If fraud is established, then a court of the lowest tier can cancel even the judgment and order of the Apex court. It was held in the case of Government of Bangladesh and another vs. Mashiur Rahman and others [50 DLR(AD) 205] that: 
"It is a cardinal principle of administration of justice that no result of any judicial proceeding should be allowed to receive judicial approval from any court of law whenever it is obtained by practicing fraud upon the court; reason being fraud demolishes the very foundation of sanctity of such judicial proceeding. It is also well established principle of law that fraud vitiates all judicial proceeding. Thus contravention of the provision of law, cannot be a valid ground for allowing an order obtained by fraud to stand. When the trial court itself on consideration of the materials on record was satisfied that a fraud had been committed in obtaining the ex parte decree it was the duty of the trial court to set aside the ex parte decree." 

22. Abdul Jalil and others vs. Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd and others reported in 64 DLR(AD) (2012) 107 as follows: 
"It is true that fraud vitiates everything; even a judgment and decree affirmed by the apex Court of the country can be declared illegal and void by the trial Court if it is proved that the judgment and decree was obtained by practicing fraud upon Court." 

23. The question is whether there was fraud in the execution and registration of the Kabala nos. 7321 and 7322 of 1977 and our answer from the above discussions is a negation. Hence, our considered view is that ordering portion of the trial court dated 27.02.1997 so far it relates the declaration of the registered Kabala nos. 7321 of 1977 and 7322 of 1977 as void, illegal, without consideration in pursuance of its order of cancellation of judgment and decree of the other suit no. 23 of 1977 be set aside.  

24. On appreciation and sifting of evidences adduced trial court disbelieved the defendant's version of cases regarding their title and possession over the suit land and we observed that appellate court with-out discarding the findings based on strong evidences reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court. 

25. Accordingly, we find merit in submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants. 

26. Accordingly, this civil appeal is disposed of. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is modified. Other Suit No.54 of 1976 subsequently renumbered as Other Suit No.61 of 1990 so far as it relates to the decree for Specific Performance of Contract is allowed. The ordering portion of the trial Court dated 27.02.1997 so far as it relates to ২৩/৭৭ নং মোকদ্দমার রায় ডিক্রী এতদ্বারা বাতিল ক্রমে উক্ত ডিক্রী মূলে ৩/৪ নং বিবাদী বরাবর ১নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক সম্পাদিত ৭৩২১ এবং ৭৩২২ নং কবলা অবৈধ, বেআইনী পনশূন্য ঘোষনা করা হইল। This portion of the judgment is set aside. 

27. The trial Court is directed to take appropriate steps for title deed in favour of the plaintiff in accordance with law. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman J.: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order .dated 12.12.2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2256 of 1998 discharging the Rule and hereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 31.05.1998 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No.48 of 1988 passed by the subordinate Judge (Artha Rim) Adalat, Dinajpur reversing the judgment and decree dated 31.05.1998 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Dinajpur and allowing Miscellaneous Case No.135 of 1983 (pre-emption). 

2. Facts leading, to filing of this, civil appeal, in short, are that 9.27 acres of land including the case land measuring 4.28 acres in plot No.1 of the pre-emption application of Cadastral Survey (in short, C.S.) Khatian No.57 and 40 decimals of land of C.S. Khatian No.185 appertaining to a combine Jama of Revisional Survey (in short, R.S.) recorded in the said C.S. Khatian Nos.57 and 185 of Mouza Umarpoil and 5.84 acres of land including case land measuring 0.84 acres of land Plot No.2 of the said application appertained to a jama of R.S. recorded in C.S. Khatian No.49 of said Mouza Umarpoil. The lands of the said holdings were in ownership of Jahangir Sarker who died leaving two sons opposite party No.6, Jasimuddin Sarker and opposite party No.7, Nasiddin alias Nasiruddin Shah of the pre-emption case; the two daughters Ayesha Bibi @ Alna Bibi and Sahabi Bibi. Sahabi Bibi died leaving behind her husband, Masiruddin and son, the pre-emptor, Shaher Ali. Masiruddin died leaving behind his 2nd wife opposite party No.11, Amisa Khatoon and her sons opposite party Nos.8-10 of the pre-emption case and 1st wife's son, the pre-emptor. 

3. The further case of the pre-emptor is that Ramesh Bhattacharja got the case lands by mortgage decree and his name was recorded as a co-sharer in State Acquisition (in short, S.A.) Khatian Nos.63, 193 and 55 exhibit Nos.3, 3(ka) and 3(kha) respectively. On his death, his six sons exchanged the case lands to opposite party No.3, Fatema Khatoon by an exchange registered deed dated 17.04.1963. The said opposite party No.3, Fatema Khatoon on execution of agreement of sale dated 02.10.1963 sold 5.12 acres of land in favour of pre-emptee opposite party. No.1, Nurul Sarker since deceased and pre-emptee opposite party No.2, Md. Serajul Karim Shah since deceased for a consideration of Tk.6,000/-; received Baina of Tk.4,000/-. Opposite party No.3 having subsequently transferred the case land to opposite party Nos.6 and 7 by sale deeds dated 01.10.1964 vide exhibits-B(3), B(6) for Tk.7,500/-, the pre-emptee opposite party No.1, Dr. Nurul Huq. Sarker and opposite party No.2, Md. Serajul Karim Shah instituted Other Class Suit No.266 of 1967 in the Court of Sadar 2nd Munsif, Dinajpur for Specific Performance of Contract of sale dated 02.10.1963 against the said opposite party No.3, Fatema Khatoon impleading her husband, Md. Ormar Ali and her son Mahatabuddin and the sub-sequent purchasers opposite party Nos.6 and 7, Jasimuddin Shahand Nasirudin Shah got contested decree dated 29.05.1968 against the said defendant and execution of the decree in Other Class Execution Case No.7 of 1983 got sale deed of the case land executed and registered through Court and got delivery of possession of the case land on 29.07.1983. 

4. The pre-emptees filing written objection contended that the pre-emption case was collusively and fraudulently brought by the subsequent purchasers opposite party 14os.6 and 7 in the name of their sister's son, Md. Shaher Ali as pre-emtor to deprive any how the pre-emptees who succeed to get sale deed of the case land after prolonged litigation upto High Court Division for about 16 years at huge expense. The pre-emptor was not a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding, his application for pre-emption was malafide, barred by limitation, principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence and bad for non joinder of necessary parties. The pre-emptor is full sister's son of the subsequent transferees opposite party Nos.6 and 7 and his father was domesticated son-in-law and on the death of his mother in his boyhood he was maintained and given in marriage by them. The contract of sale by opposite party No.3, Fatema Khatoon of the case land in favour of the pre-empteess took place in presence of the pre-emptor and his said maternal uncle. The pre-emptor and his maternal uncle opposite party Nos.6 and 7 refused to purchase the case land and consented to and actively negotiated the sale by opposite party No to the pre-emptees opposite party Nos.1 and 2 making them agreeable to purchase. 

5. It was further contended that the pre-emptor and the opposite party Nos.3-7 subsequently created collusive deeds of sale dated 01.10.1964 in respect of the case lands, exhibits-B(3), B(6) by the opposite party No.3 in favour of opposite party Nos.6 and 7 to frustrate agreement of sale dated 02.10.1963. But they were not bonafide transferee for valuable consideration. Other Class suit No. 266 of 1967 for specific performance of contract of sale was decreed on 29.05.1968 on contest. They appealed against the decree being Other Class Appeal No.65 of 1968 which was dismissed on contest on 30.08.1980. The Opposite party Nos.6 and 7 did not stop there and made application under Sections 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Nigh Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.1576 of 1980 which was discharged on 03.11.1982. Thereafter, the decree holders act gale deed No.1757 under pre-emption executed and registered through Court on 05.06.1983 and delivery of possession of the case land through Court in Other Class Execution Case Mo.7 of 1983. Finding no other alternative way to deprive the pre-emptees of the case land fraudulent and collusively the pre-emption case was started by the opposite party Nos.6 and 7 with their money in the name of their sister's son as pre-emptor after 20 years of the agreement of sale by the opposite party No.3 when the value of the case land was at least Tk.1 lac. 

6. It also contended that the pre-emption case was not maintainable and the pre-emptor had no locus standi to pre-empt the sale made in execution of the decree for specific performance or contract of sale and that with the publication of the S.A. Khatian creating separate holdings under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act repealing the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, application for pre; emption under Section 96 of the said-Act on the basis of C.S. Khatian and Jama mentioned therein was under Section 96 of the Act could not be made applicable retrospectively and further that the owner of the case land Ramesh Chandra Bhattacharja having got mutation of Jama for the case land at Tk. 15.00 and separate khatian No.57/1 for the case land having been published in his name in which the pre-emptor was not a sharer tenant and in the kabala under preemption, the said khatian No.57/1 having been mentioned as Khatian of the case land, the preemptor had no locus standi to maintain the application. Further that without deposit of taka one lac as prevailing value of the case land on 05.06.1983 with compensation and costs of litigation incurred by the pre-emptee the preemption case was bad for insufficient deposit. The application was also bad for defect of parties as the sons of Ramesh Chandra Bhattacharja and the heirs of recorded tenant Nomir Mohammad were necessary parties in the case of the pre-emptor on the face of S.A. Khatian as exhbit-3 series but were not impleaded and, as such, the said miscellaneous case (pre-emption) is liable to be set aside. 

7. The trial Court dismissed the case in favour of the defendants by the judgment and decree dated 31.05.1988. 

8. On appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No.48 of 1988, the appellate Court allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court by the judgment and order dated 31.05.1998. 

9. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree dated 31.05.1998 passed by the Sub-Judge (Artha) Adatal, Dinajpur, the defendant-respondents as petitioners preferred Civil Revision No .2256 of 1998 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule. 

10. In due course, a single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties discharged the Rule by the impugned judgment and order dated 12.12.2004. 

11. Feeling aggrieved, by the impugned judgment and order dated 12.12.2004 passed by the High Court Division, the defendant as petitioners filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.388 of 2005 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal. 

12. Mr. Mansur Habib, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the High Court Division perusing the Lower Court's Records and consequently upon non-consideration of the material evidence particularly the operative portion of the document under pre-emption showing the case land appertaining to holding of S.A. Khatian No.57/1 the home of Ramesh Chandra Bhattacharja on the basis of mutation in which the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer wrongly found that the pre-emptee petitioners could not prove that Jama of case Khatians were separated and separate Khatians were prepared so as to disown the claims of the pre-emptor as co-sharer of the lands of the case Khatian and the High Court Division failed to advert to the grounds taken in Revisional application that the Courts below committed error in the decision occasioning failure of justice failing to appreciate that because of the repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act with the publication of S.A. Khatian under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, prayer for Preemption under section 96 of the later Act as made on the basis of C.S. Khatian published under Bengal Tenancy Act no longer in force as not maintainable inasmuch as the provision and purport of section 96 of the Act could not be given retrospective application to the instant sale long after repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act. He further submits that the High Court Division upon non-consideration of iota of material evidence failed to appreciate that, the principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence would operate from the date of contract of sale on 02.10.1963 taking place in presence of and through active negotiation of the pre-emptor and his maternal uncle opposite party Nos.6 and 7 wrongly concurred with the finding of the Appellate Court that the pre-emption case was not barred by the principle of waiver, estoppels and acquiescence and to appreciate that the pre-emption case was bad for non-joinder of necessary parties as categorically pointed out in the grounds of revisional application. He next submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate on consideration of evidence of collusive and fraudulent nature and character of the pre-emption case brought by his maternal uncles, opposite party Nos.6 and 7 of the pre-emption case failing to succeed on contest as sub-sequent transferees of the case land in the suit for specific performance of contract of sale litigating up to High Court Division. He finally submits that the pre-emption case was not maintainable by deposit of consideration of Tk.6,000/- on the basis of agreement dated 02.10.1963 when evidence of P.W.1, the pre-emptor and other evidence show the value of the case land on the date of the deed executed through Court was at least taka on Lac and, as such, impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 

13. No one appears on behalf of the respondents. 

14. We have heard the learned Advocate for the appellants. Perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

15. Before entering into the merit of the appeal, it would be relatable to get through the grounds, for which, leave was granted. The grounds are quoted below: 
"Mr. Nazibar Rahman, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners submits that the High Court Division perusing the Lower Court's Records and consequently upon non-consideration of the material evidence particularly the operative portion of the document under pre-emption showing the case lands appertaining to holding of S.A. Khatian No.57/1 the home of Ramesh Chandra Bhattacharja on the basis of mutation in which the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer wrongly found that the pre-emptee petitioners could not prove that Jama of case Khatian were separated and separate Khatians were prepared so as to dis-own the claims of the pre-emptor as co-sharer of the lands of the case Khatian and the High Court Division failed to advert to the grounds taken in Revisional application that the Courts below committed error in the decision occasioning failure of jus-tice failing to appreciate that because of the repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act with the publication of S.A. Khatian under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act prayer for Pre-emption under Section 96 of the later Act as made on the basis of C.S. Khatian published under Bengal Tenancy Act no longer in force was not maintainable inasmuch as the provision and purport of 96 of the Act could not be given retrospective application to the instant sale long after repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act. 
The learned Advocate further submits that the High Court Division upon non-consideration of iota of material evidence failed to appreciate that the principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence would operate from the date of contract of sale on 02.10:1963 taking place in presence of and through active negotiation of the preemptor and his maternal uncle opposite party Nos.6 and 7 wrongly concurred with the finding of the appellate Court that the pre-emption case was not barred by the principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence and to appreciate that the pre-emption case was bad for non-joinder of necessary parties as categorically pointed out in the grounds of revisional application. He further submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate on consideration of evidence of collusive and fraudulent nature and character of the preemption case brought by his maternal uncles opposite party Nos. 6 and 7 of the pre-emption case failing to succeed on contest as subsequent transferrees of the case lands in the suit for specific performance of contract of sale litigating up to High Court Division. Lastly, he submits that the pre-emption case was not maintainable by deposit of consideration of TK.6,000.00 on the basis of agreement dated 02.10.1963 when evidence of PW-1, the pre-emptor and other evidence show the value of the case lands on the date of the deed executed through Court was at least taka one Lac." 

16. In this case, the lower Appellate Court arrived at finding that the pre-emptor Md. Saher Ali was a co-sharer by inheritance of the case holding, the case was not barred by limitation and also not bad from having defect of parties. In addition, the High Court Division too concurred with these findings of the Courts below. 

17. It is the long standing prime principle of appreciation of evidence that finding of facts, arrived at by the lower Appellate Court is immune from interference in revisional jurisdiction, apart from in certain well definite circumstances such as non-consideration and misreading of material evidence affecting the merit of the case, or misconception, misapplication or misapprehension of law. 

18. On perusal of the materials on record, our considered view in these ends is that, the Appellate Court as well as the High Court Division have correctly arrived at these decisions and there were no misconception, misapplication or misapprehension of legal scheme of the matters in question which clearly affects the merit of the case and made miscarriage of justice, as well as violation of principle of law. 

19. The sole point on which the Appellate Court parts with the findings of the Trial Court is that on principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The Trial Court finds that the pre-emptor was barred by application of the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence and the Appellate Court on the basis of case law decided by this Division in the case of Fazaruddin vs. Maijuddin and others reversed the judgment of the trial Court which was reported to the 44 DLR (AD)62 which runs as follows: 
"It is true, the right of pre-emption accrues after transfer of the land and statutory right of pre-emption cannot be taken away by mere verbal assurance of the person having such right unless other facts and circumstances clearly make out a case of acquiescence or waiver. 'Acquiescence' arises when a person, knowing that he is entitled to enforce some right, neglects to do so for such a long time that the other person opposing such right may fairly infer that he has waived or abandoned it. It is failure to object to certain transaction or Act. "Waiver" means simply abandonment of any claim or right." 

20. The same view was maintained in the case of Md. Dewan Ali Vs Md. Jasimuddin and others, 13 MLR (AD) 198 and reiterated in the case of Shamsun Nahar and Ors. vs. Abdur Noon: and Ors. reported in LEX/ BDAD/0300/2015. 

21. On the discussion of finding of facts arrived at by the Appellate Court as Well as the High Court Division, we find no basis to reopen the matter and take a diametrically opposed view on the question on which leave was granted. Because, the evidence on record does not expressly support the case of negotiation of the sale to the pre-emptor, rather, the trial Court's discussions were beyond, the principles of the above referred case law. 

22. For itself, this Division find no non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence on record or an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice or such, finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law or misconception, misapplication or misapprehension of law in the judgment and order of the High Court Division. 

23. We find no substance in all of the contentions raised by the learned Counsel for the appellants. The High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision. We, therefore, find no reason to interfere with the same. 

24. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque, J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 26-1-2020 passed by the Joint District Judge 1st Court, Bogura in Miscellaneous Case No. 151 of 2019 filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure rejecting the same.
2. Facts of the case, in brief, are that, the respondent Nos. 1-4 as plaintiff, filed Partition Suit No. 289 of 2013 against the present appellant as defendant No. 25 along with other defendants. The appellant contesting the suit by filing written statement. The suit was fixed for settling date on 17-9-2017. On t1 date fixed the plaintiff filed an application for fixing the suit for peremptory hearing which was allowed by the court on 6-3-2018 and fixed the suit for peremptory hearing on 8-5-2018, but the appellant claims that the plaintiff did not serve any copy of such application to his lawyer and without informing the fact of filing the application they proceeded with the hearing of the suit and finally got the ex-parte decree on 23-7-2017. The present appellant filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree. The miscellaneous case was contested by the plaintiffs in suit by filing written objection. The trial court by impugned order dated 26-1-2020 rejected the same awarding costs of Taka 5,000 to the opposite party, hence, the present appeal.
3. Mr Md Sultan Uddin with Mosammat Morsheda Parvin, learned Advocates appearing for the Appellant submits that the conducting lawyer for the defendant No. 25 was entrusted with the task of taking day to day step in the suit and one of his employee was looking after the case on his behalf, but at a point of time the “কার্যকারক” of the defendant No. 25 met an accident consequently, he could not communicate with the learned Advocate as well as the learned Advocate also did not inform about the position of the suit and did not take any step on behalf of the defendant, resultantly, the suit was decreed ex-parte.
4. He further submits that for default of the pleader of the defendant appellant the party should not suffer and it was the duty of the learned Advocate to attend the court regularly and take proper steps on his behalf as such, the appellant has sufficient cause for restoration of the suit in its original number and position by setting aside the ex-parte decree.
5. He further submits that the suit was at the stage of settling date when the plaintiffs filed an application for fixing the date from settling date to peremptory hearing, therefore, they ought to have served the copy of the application upon the learned Advocate for the defendants, but without service of copy the trial court unilaterally fixed the date for peremptory hearing, as such, the ex-parte decree is liable to be set-aside. In support of his such submissions he has referred to the cases of Government of Bangladesh and another vs Mashiur Rahman and others reported in 50 DLR (AD)205, Kabir Ahmed Sawdagar vs Md Syed Saifuddin Jaheed and others, reported in 58 DLR 277 and Malkiat Singh and another vs Joginder Singh and others reported in 2 SCC 206.
6. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing for the Respondent Nos. 1-4 submits that the appellant, as defendant No. 25 filed written statement in the suit but on all subsequent dates he did not take any step in the suit. Moreover, after fixing the suit for peremptory hearing on 8-5-2018, the plaintiff took adjournment on 8-7-2018 and thereafter, the suit was fixed for hearing on 9-4-2019, 28-5-2019 and finally fixed for ex-parte hearing on 8-7-2019, but on all dates the defendant took no step either by filing hazira or seeking adjournment of the hearing consequently, the trial court had no order alternative but to proceed with the hearing of the suit and decreed the suit decreed ex-parte.
7. He finally submits that the trial court while rejecting the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code rightly observed that the defendant No. 25 and his lawyer very negligently' dealt with the matter and failed to appear when the suit was fixed for hearing on repeated calls, as such, the trial court by rejecting the miscellaneous case has not committed any illegality in law. Moreover, after passing the preliminary decree the court appointed an Advocate Commissioner for effecting the partition who submitted report and the preliminary decree has been made final, as such, there is no scope for interfering with the decree passed by the trial court.
8. Heard the learned Advocates for both the parties, have gone through the memo of appeal, application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code, ex-parte decree dated 23-7-2019 passed by the trial court and the impugned judgment and order of the court below.
9. Admittedly, the respondent Nos. 1-4, as plaintiffs, instituted Partition Suit No. 289 of 2013 in the court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Bogura praying for a decree of partition of the suit property. The appellant, as defendant No. 25, entered into appearance and filed written statement. It is also found that the suit was fixed on 17-9-2017 for SD and on that date the plaintiffs filed an application praying for fixing the suit for peremptory hearing without service of any copy to the learned advocate of the defendant.
10. However, the defendant-appellant ought to have followed the cause list of the court day to day and up-to-date position of the suit, but the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 25 failed to discharge his duty consequently, the suit was decreed ex-parte. Learned Advocate for the appellant contended that it is the fault of the learned conducting lawyer for the defendant-appellant and for which the defendant cannot be penalized in anyway and negligence of an advocate is sufficient cause for filing an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code for setting aside ex-parte decree. He finally submits that had the defendant appellant served the application filed by the plaintiffs for fixing the case for hearing and the learned Advocate informed the appellant, he would have contested the suit by deposing on his behalf, but because of negligence of the learned Advocate as well as non-service of copy of the application filed by the plaintiff the defendant could not know about fixing of the date for peremptory hearing.
11. On the other hand, learned Advocate for the respondent contended that the defendant knowing fully well about fixing of the case for peremptory hearing did not take any step and allowed the plaintiffs to get the decree ex-parte and filing of the miscellaneous case is only to harass the plaintiffs and to drag the matter for years together to the detriment of the plaintiffs, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed.
12. To appreciate submission of the learned Advocate for the parties, this Court have gone through the ex-parte decree dated 23-7-2019 passed by the trial court in Partition Suit No. 289 of 2013 which run thus:
“অদ্য একতরফা আদেশ এর জন্য দিন ধার্ধ্য আছে। বাদীপক্ষ হাজিরা দাখিল করিয়াছে। নথি পেশ করা হইল । নথি একতরফা আদেশের জন্য নেওয়া হইল । অত্র মামলার নথি, প্রদত্ত সাক্ষ্য ও দাখিলীয় কাগজপত্র পর্যালোচনা করলাম । নথি পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় বাদী তাহার মোকদ্দমাটি একতরফা ভাবে মৌখিক ও দালিলিক সাক্ষ্য দ্বারা প্রমাণ করিতে সক্ষম হইয়াছে । সার্বিক পর্যালোচনায় মামলাটি, একতরফা সূত্রে প্রমাণিত । এমতাবস্থায় বাদী প্রার্থিত মতে প্রতিকার পাইতে হকদার ।
প্রদত্ত কোর্ট ফি সঠিক
অতএব
আদেশ হয় যে,
অত্র মোকদ্দমাটি বিবাদীপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে একতরফা বিচারে বিনা খরচায় ডিক্রী দেওয়া হইল । বাদীপক্ষ দাবীকৃত নালিশী তফশীল বর্ণিত ০.০৪ শতক জমি বাবদ বন্টনের প্রাথমিক ডিক্রী প্রাপ্ত হইল।
ডিক্রীকৃত জমি আগামী ৬০ দিনের মধ্যে বাদী বরাবর বন্টন করে দিতে বিবাদীপক্ষকে নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইল । ব্যর্থতায় বাদীপক্ষ আদালত যোগে বন্টন করে নিতে পারিবে।”
<u>13. Now, the question has arisen whether the decree passed ex-parte by the trial court in a partition suit is in conformity with the provisions of Order XX, rule 5 of the Code which provides that "judgment of the courts shall contain a concise statement of the case, the points for determination, the decision thereon and the reasons for such decision, but the judgment passed ex-parte by the trial court as quoted herein above seems to be not a judgment in accordance with Order XX, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This is a judgment written by the trial court in a very slipshod manner and contrary to the provisions of Order XX, rule 5. Code of Civil Procedure does not define either an ex-parte judgment or an ex-parte decree. It refers only to a judgment and a decree. In the event a judgment is known to be an ex-parte judgment and decree drawn on the basis of that judgment is known as an ex-parte decree. Hence, even of an ex-parte judgment and the decree, the basic ingredients of judgment must be available to the extent to indicate that the court has applied its mind to the pleading, relief claimed thereunder, the evidence and conclusion arrived at by the court on the above.</u>
14. Apart from negligence of the learned Advocate for the defendant, the court below did not observe the minimum legal requirement as provided in Order XX, rule 5 of the Code, as such, on that count also the ex-parte judgment is not at all sustainable in law.
15. The trial court while rejecting the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure instead of discussing the case of the applicant whether he was prevented by sufficient cause or whether before fixing the suit for peremptory hearing, the plaintiff served any copy of the application upon the learned Advocate for the defendant. This court finds no reflection in the impugned judgment and order about the points mentioned above.
<u>16. In view of the above, this Court finds that the ex-parte decree passed by the trial court not only suffers from minimum legal requirement under Order XX, rule 5 of the Code, but also erroneous because of the fact that the court in rejecting the application utterly failed to observe the requirement for restoration of any suit by setting aside an ex-parte decree, as such, the judgment and order appealed against is liable to be set-aside.</u>
17. Taking into consideration the above, this Court finds merit in the appeal as well as in the submissions of the learned advocate for the appellant.
18. In the result, the appeal is allowed. Judgment and order of the trial court is hereby set-aside along with all other subsequent steps and final decree as all the subsequent steps taken by the trial court during subsistence of stay order of this Court.
19. The Partition Suit No. 289 of 2013 is hereby restored in its original number and position. The trial court is hereby directed to dispose of the suit within 6 (six) months from the date of receipt of this judgment without allowing any unreasonable adjournment to the parties to the proceeding, in particular, to the defendant-appellant.
20. Connected Civil Rule No. 102 (FM) of 2020 is also disposed of herewith.
21. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated. There will be no order as to costs.
Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concerned at once.
End.
