full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan, J: This Civil Appeal by leave granting order dated 24-7-2008 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal NoA25 of 2007 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 10-5-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3151 of 1998 discharging the Rule affirming the judgment and decree dated 4-2-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhaii in Title Appeal No.101 of 1982 dismissing the appeal affirming the judgment and decree dated 22-6-1982 passed by the learned Munsif 3rd Court, Sadar, Noakhali in her Class Suit No.201 of 1980 decreeing the suit.
2. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of this Civil Appeal are in a mutshell, that the predecessor of the respondents No.1(a)-1(g), Md Rafiquzzaman Bhuiyan as plaintiff filed the Other Class Suit No.201 of 1980 on 12-11-1980 for declaration of title over "Kha' schedule land and later on after amendment prayed for recovery of Khas possession by evicting the defendants No. 8-10 from the suit land as appended to the plaint stating, inter alia, that the father of plaintiff Md Rafiquzzaman Bhuiyan and the pro-forma defendants No.2-6, namely Alhaj Ali Azam purchased 0.22 acres of land by Kabala dated 10-2-1953 from Kailash Chandra Bhuiyan, Khetra Mohan Bhuiyan and Botu Keshar Bhuiyan in the Benami of pro-forma defendant No.7. Said Alhaj Ali Azam died leaving behind the plaintiff Md Rafiquzzaman Bhuiyan and the pro-forma defendants No.2-6 as sons and daughters. The plaintiff got the suit "Kha' schedule land by amicable partition with pro-forma defendants No. 2-6 and since the date of Kabala the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land. On 1240-1980 the plaintiff came to know that the suit land has been recorded in Khas Khatian in the name of the defendant No. l. The defendant No.1 is trying to lease out the suit land. By a subsequent amendment to the plaint the plaintiff further claimed that during the pendency of the suit the defendants No.8-10 forcibly entered into the suit land on 18-11-1980 and constructed a tin-shed structure although they were not entitled to enter into or construct any house in the suit land.
3. The government as defendant No.1 contested the said suit by filing written statement, contending, inter alia, that the suit land is government Khas land and is part of the Bazar namely Zamindar Hat. The said land has been recorded in Khas Khatian No.1 during SA and MRR operation, All the Bazars became khas land and were vested to the government from 1st Baishak 1368 BS as per The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the government has been leasing out the said Bazar since 1368 BS Accordingly during preparation of MRR Kkatian the same has been recorded as Hat in the name of the Government, The plaintiff never possessed the suit land and, as such, he has no right, title or interest over the suit land, hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. The suit land is being possessed by the defendant No. 7, who constructed a grocery shop thereon and subsequently applied for lease of the Suit land.
4. The plaintiff examined four witnesses as PWs 1-4 while the defendant No. l adduced one witness as DW 1. The plaintiff filed the documents which had been marked as Exhibits 1-3, on the other hand, those filed by the defendant No. l had been marked as Exhibits A and B.
5. The trial Court on completion of the trial decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 22-6-1982. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the trial Court the defendant No. l preferred Title Appeal No. 101 of 1982 and on transfer the said appeal was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhali and dismissed the same by judgment and decree dated 4-2-1996. Thereafter, the defendant No.1 as petitioner filed Civil Revision No. 3151 of 1998 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree dated 4-2-1996 passed by the appellate Court and Rule was issued. Upon final hearing the High Court Division was pleased to discharge the Rule by the judgment and decree dated 10- 5-2006.
6. Being disgruntled with the judgment and decree dated 10-5-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3151 of 1998 the defendant No.1-appellant preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before this Division and leave was granted, hence the instant appeal.
7. Mr Md Taherul Islam, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellant has taken us through the judgment and decree of the High Court Division dated 10-5-2006 passed in Civil Revision No.3151 of 1998, judgment and decree of trial Court as well as appellate Court, the other materials on record and contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the petitioner upon misreading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby misdirected beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous discharging the Rule absolute occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. The learned Counsel for the appellant contends next that the all the courts below failed to appreciate that the suit land is the land of Hat belonging to the government and the same is in possession of the government from a long time. Accordingly, the suit land was recorded in the name of the government in MRR and BS Khatian. The learned Counsel argues next that the government has been possessing the suit land through the defendant No.7, who constructed a grocery shop thereon and subsequently applied for taking lease of the suit land, but all the Courts below did not consider the said facts. The learned Counsel submits further that the appellate Court in its judgment mentioned that C-1, C-2 and D files of the original suit has been destroyed from the record room of the learned District Judge and the parties were directed to file documents including the copy of oral evidence, but the parties did not file any copy of oral evidence yet the appellate Court affirmed the judgment of trial Court and thereafter the High Court Division also upheld the judgment of appellate Court and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division is liable to be scraped.
8. Per contra, Mr Probir Neogi, senior Advocate along with Mr Shishir Kanti Mazumder, Advocate and Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, Advocate has refuted the arguments adduced by the appellant. The learned Counsels contend that all the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff has title in the suit land which according to law cannot be interfered with by this Division. The learned Counsels submit next that the government-appellant failed to prove that Hat is situated on the suit land and the same was leased out at the relevant time. The learned Counsels submit further that the findings of fact arrived by the Courts below being based on record calls for no interference by this Division and hence the instant appeal is liable to be dismissed.
9. We have perused the judgment and decree dated 10-5-2006 passed in Civil Revision No.3151 of 1998. We have also considered the submissions of the learned Counsel for both sides and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court, evidences and other materials on record.
10. At the threshold, let us see how the plaintiff has been able to prove his title in the suit land. The plaintiff claims that his father purchased the suit land in Benami of the defendant No.7 from Kailsha Chandra Bhuiyan and others by way of Sale Deed dated 10-2-1953. It appears that the plaintiff filed original copy of the said deed which was marked as Exhibit-1. The said deed being thirty years old has presumptive value regarding its genuineness. It is advantageous to discuss section 90 of the Evidence Act, 1872 which is extracted in the following:
"90 Presumption as to documents thirty years old—Where any document, purporting or proved to be thirty years old, is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper the Court may presume that the signature and every other part of such document which purports to be in the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person's handwriting and in the case of a document executed or attested, that it was duly executed and attested by the persons by whom it purports to be executed and attested.
Explanation—Documents are said to be in proper custody if they are in the place in which, and under the care of the person with whom, they would naturally be; but no custody is improper if it is proved to have had a legitimate origin, or if the circumstances of the particular case are such as to render such an origin probable."
<u><u>11. In view of section 90 of the Evidence Act, 1872 and the context of the case in hand it is evident that the said sale deed (Exhibit 1) has got a presumptive value to the effect that the same is genuine deed inasmuch as the deed was produced from the proper custody of the plaintiff. On the other hand, the defendant No.1 has not been able to impinge on the genuineness of the said sale deed either by oral evidence or documentary evidence. The trial Court as well as the appellate Court and finally the High Court Division concurrently found the said sale deed as true and genuine.</u></u>
12. Again, on plain reading of DS Khatian No.58 (Exhibit 3) it appears that the suit plot No.2141 was recorded in the name of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff's father named Swarup Chandra Bhuiyan from whom the plaintiff's father purchased the suit land in benami of the defendant No.7. It also appears from the Exhibit-3 that the nature of the suit land had been described in DS Khatian as orchard'. Had the suit land been part of Hat then it should have been written to the same effect. The plaintiff claimed that he used to cut down the trees on the suit land from time to time and for the said reason the suit land was vacant land. PW 2 also stated in his deposition that the suit land was orchard. In the similar way, PW 3 deposed supporting the deposition of PWs 1 and 2 regarding the said assertion. It was argued on behalf of the defendant No.1 that the suit land being in close proximity to a Bazaar and said Bazaar had later on extended to the suit land. But the said claim of the defendant No.1 was not supported by the evidence on record. On the other hand, it is settled principle of law that mere recording of the suit land in the name of the defendant No.1 without proof of title does not devolve any ownership of the suit land upon the defendant No. l. In the light of the discussion made above, it is crystal clear that the plaintiff has title and possession of the suit land prior to dispossession on 18-11-1980.
13. On perusal of Advocate Commissioner's Report available on the record it is evident that on 18-11-1980 the defendants No.8. 10 intruded into the suit land and made some construction. Thus, it is found that during the pendency of the suit the plaintiff had been dispossessed from the suit land on 18-11-1980.
14. In view of the foregoing discussion, the trial Court on proper appraisal of the oral evidence as well as documentary evidence available on the record decreed the suit. The appellate Court and the High Court Division also most legally upheld the judgment and decree of the trial Court. We do not find any perversion in the impugned judgment and decree and, as such, we are impelled to hold that the plaintiff has acquired a valid title and possession in the suit land and during the pendency of suit the plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendants No.8-10. Due to reasons stated above, it does not warrant interference with the judgment and decree dated 10-5-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3151 of 1998. Therefore, we do not find any merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant and, as such, the instant Civil Appeal is liable to be dismissed.
Consequently, the instant Civil Appeal is dismissed.
End.

full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 21.01.2019 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3877 of 2017 making the Rule absolute with direction. 

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the civil petition are that the petitioner herein as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.199 of 2000 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Barishal Sadar, Barishal, for declaration of title in the suit land which was decreed ex-parte vide judgment and decree dated 03.10.2004. 

3. Challenging the ex-parte decree, the defendant no.1 of the suit filed Miscellaneous Case No.75 of 2004 for set-ting aside the ex-parte decree under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that no summons has been served upon him. The Trial Court rejected the miscellaneous case vide judgment and order dated 28.10.2013. 

4. Having aggrieved, defendant-respondent no.1 filed Miscellaneous Appeal No.70 of 2013 in the Court of learned District Judge, Barishal, which on transfer was heard by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Barishal, who after hearing the parties disallowed the appeal by judgment and order dated 23.07.2017.
 
5. Being dissatisfied, the defendant-respondent no.1 moved before the High Court Division by filing an application under Section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure which was numbered as Civil Revision No.3877 of 2017. 

6. Upon hearing the parties, a Single Bench of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute with direction vide judgment and order dated 21.01.2019 holding that Order V Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not complied with in serving the notice upon the defendant no. 1. 

7. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied with impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiff-respondent as petitioner filed this civil petition for leave to appeal invoking Article 103 of the Constitution. 

8. Mr. Zulfiqur Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing on of the petitioner submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that in compliance with the provision of Order V Rule 19 (B) of the Code of Civil Procedure summons was duly served upon the defendant and this finding was also concurred by both the courts below as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

9. On the other hand Mr. Sk. Mohammad Morshed, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent no.1 in support of the impugned judgment and order submits that though both the trial court and appellate court below observed in their judgment that notices were received by the defendant nos.2 and 5 on behalf of all the defendants but Order V Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure mandates that where there are more defendant than one, service of the summons shall be made on each defendants. He also referring Rule 04 of Order XX of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding judgment of the courts below submits that the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 03.10.2004 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Barishal Sadar, Barishal, in Title Suit No.199 of 2000 is not a proper judgment as mandate in the above mentioned Rule and Order as such there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division. 

10. However, both the learned Advocates for the parties admits that the main suit for declaration of title should be determined on merit in accordance with law. 

11. On the submissions made above by the learned Advocate for the parties, we are of the view that justice would be best served, if the issues of the Title Suit No.199 of 2000 are adjudicated on merit in accordance with law. 

12. Accordingly, the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3877 of 2017 is modified by expunging the words "with Tk. 10,000/-" and the sentence "the petitioner is directed to pay a fine of Tk. 10,000/- to the opposite party no.1 within 30 (thirty) days from receipt of this order". 

13. Consequently, impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is modified by expunging the words and sentence stated above with the following direction: 
"The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Barishal Sadar, Barishal, is hereby directed to dispose of the Title Suit No.199 of 2000 on merit in accordance with law within 06 (Six) months from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment and order." 

14. Accordingly, this civil petition is disposed of. 

15. Communicate a copy of this judgment and order at once. 

16. No order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman J. This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 13.12.2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4504 of 2004 making the Rule absolute modifying the judgment and order dated 20.11.2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Miscellaneous Appeal No.04 of 2003 affirming the judgment and order dated 15.02.2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No.103 of 2002 without disposing the application for injunction filed by the defendant No.3 against the plaintiffs in which show cause notice was issued on 8-5-2003. 

2. Facts, leading to filing this civil appeal, is short, are that plaintiffs as petitioners herein instituted Title Suit No.103 of 2002 in the 1ST Court of Joint District Judge, Gazipur praying for declaration that the judgment and decree of Title Suit No.298 of 1980 was not binding upon the plaintiffs. They also filed an application on 19.11.2002 under Order 39, Rule I read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for temporary injunction against the defendant restraining them from entering into the suit land by force or from constructing boundary wall or cutting away trees from the suit land. The trial court by order dated 09.11.2002 issued notice upon the defendants and ad-interim injunction was also passed not to disturb the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs. Defendant No.1 appeared in the suit and filed written objection against the prayer for temporary injunction of the plaintiff on 15.02.2003 and the trial court after hearing the parties vacated the order of ad-interim injunction. Being aggrieved the plaintiff petitioners preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.4 of 2003, which was heard by the 1st Court of the learned Additional District Judge, Gazipur and the appeal was dismissed. But the defendant No.3 (Zahid Maleque respondent No.1 in this petition) filed an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court Division against the aforesaid judgment and order of the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur dated 20.11.2004 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No.04 of 2003 and the said application was registered as Civil Revision No.4504 of 2004 and rule was issued against present petitioners. The High Court Division by impugned judgment and order dated 13.12.2004 made the rule absolute. Plaintiff-petitioners and defendant opposite party No.5 i.e. the Deputy Commissioner, Gazipur and their agents have been restrained by an order of ad-interim injunction from interfering with the possession of defendant No.3 (i.e. respondent No.1 in the suit property in any manner till disposal of Title Suit No.103 of 2003. Hence is this case. 

3. The plaintiffs-petitioners feeling aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 13.12.2004 of the High Court Division preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.56 of 2005 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal. 

4. Mr. A. M. Amin Uddin, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the High Court Division issued Rule on 30.11.2004 returnable within 4(four) weeks but before expiry of the returnable date the rule was heard ex-parte on 13.12.2004 to the serious prejudice of the petitioners and, thus, the High Court Division committed an error of law. He further submits that with reference to the revisional application filed before the High Court Division that the application itself being not in form, hence, it was not maintainable and, as such, in an application which itself lacked maintainability, the High Court Division passed the impugned judgment and order at the back of the petitioners and thereby committed an error of law. The Mr. A. M. Amin Uddin then referred to the following observation of the High Court Division "Therefore we find that the learned appellate Court due to omission failed to pass any order in the petition filed by the petitioner under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code. Accordingly, we find merit in the Rule". He next submits that the impugned judgment of the High Court Division does not disclose any reasonable ground for passing the said order and, as such, it calls for interference. He further submits that the high Court Division did not consider that the suit land is the Forest Department under the Government of Bangladesh which is controlled and supervised by the Forest Department since 1950 after avulsion of Zaminder system under gazette notification dated 15.12.1953 submits that the High Court Division failed to consider in law as well as facts the possession controlled and management of the Forest Department since 1950. Now the suit land is under the guidance of Asian Development Bank (ADB) there was a share of landless peoples and after in the year 1956, nobody has no right save and accept the Forest Department and, as such, the impugned and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

5. Per contra, Dr. Kazi Akter Hamid, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos.1-2 submits in support of the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. He further submits that there is no error in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and, therefore, the instant appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

6. We have heard Mr. A. M. Amin Uddin, the learned Senior Advocate for the appellants and Dr. Kazi Akter Hamid, the learned senior Advocate for the respondents. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

7. It appears that the Divisional Forest Officer, Dhaka and 3 others of the Government preferred this appeal against the judgment and order dated 13-12-2004 passed by the High Court Division making the Rule absolute. 

8. The plaintiffs of the Title Suit No.103 of 2002 institutes the suit praying for declaration that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.298 of 1980 is not binding upon them and further prayed for declaration of title over the suit property. Pending suit, the plaintiffs as petitioners filed an application under order 39 Rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the defendants. The trial Court by order dated 09- 11-2002 issued notice with an ad-interim order of injunction. The defendants appeared in the suit and con-tested the application for injunction. The trial court after hearing the Parties vacated the ad-interim order. Hence, the plain-tiffs as appellants preferred the Miscellaneous Appeal. No.4 of 2003 in the Court of District. Judge, Gazipur which was eventually heard by the Additional District Judge, Gazipur who by his judgment and order dated 20.11.2004 Dismissed the miscellaneous appeal. 

9. The defendant No.3 unsuccessfully filed the Civil Revision being No.4504 of 2004 before the High Court Division against the said judgment and order of the Additional District Judge the High Court Division after hearing the parties made the Rule absolute restraining the opposite parties not to interfere with the possession of the defendant No.3. 

10. However, it appears that the application for temporary injunction is still pending before the trial Court. In view of the pendency of the application for injunction and suit, we are, therefore, of the view that it would be directed to maintain status quo by both the parties in respect of suit properties till final hearing of the injunction application. 

11. The trial Court, however, is directed to dispose of the injunction application expeditiously and conclude: the trial Court of the suit within 6(six) months from the date of communication of this order positively without unnecessary adjournment.

12. The appeal is accordingly disposed of. 

13. Let the copy of this judgment and order be sent to the trial Court for necessary action. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Abu Zafor Siddique J. This Civil Appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 18.08.2002 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1400 of 1997 making the Rule absolute.
2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the appellants as plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit. No. 100 of 1969 in the Court of learned Senior Munsif (now Senior Assistant Judge), Jamalpur for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of .27 V2 acme of land forming the western part of .55 acre of land appertaining to C.S. Plot No.237 of C.S. 1Chatian No.32 of Mouza-Char Roy locally known as Rayerchar of Police Station-Sadar and District-Jamalpur stating, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to one Adu Mona and after his death it devolved upon his heirs namely Sarabdi Molia, Dabaru Molla and others and the same was recorded in their names and suit plot No.237 was in the saham of aforesaid Sarabdii Molla and his brother Dabariu. Molla. Sarabdi Molia died leaving behind three sons namely Gahar Mona, Mahar Molia, Sayed Molla and a daughter who died without issue. Dabaru Molia died leaving behind son jaminuddin and two daughters. Gahar Mona died leaving behind two sons Hasen Ali, Kazim and two daughters Kuslom, Batashi. The heirs of Hagen Ali Molla and others sold the suit land to aforesaid jaminuddin and others who thereafter sold the property to the plaintiffs on 20.31.1957 and the plaintiffs gave the said land in barga to the predecessor of the defendants. Further case of the plaintiffs was that their claimed land of C.S. Plot N .737 was recorded in new plot Nos.673 and 674 and they were in possession of .27 acre in Plot No.67/1 and defendant No.1 dispossessed them from the suit land and hence, they had instituted the suit.
3. Defendant No.1 (predecessor of the respondents) contested the suit by filing a written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that Amud Molla was the owner of the suit land but it was wrongly recorded in the names of Sarabdi and others in elmali. Sarabdi and Dabaru never possessed the land. Amud Molla sold the suit land to Bakhar Molla (father of defendant No.1) on 21.07.1920 by registered kabala in which Gahar Molla (son of Sarabdi Molla) was an attesting witness. During operation of the rent roll the plaintiff unsuccessfully raised objection and as such the suit was liable to be dismissed.

4. Upon hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Jamalpur by his judgment and order dated 23.08.3995 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved defendant No.1 preferred Other Class Appeal No.76 of 1995 in the Court of learned District Judge, Jamalpur. On transfer, the appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Jamalpur, who by his judgment and order dated 10.11.1996 eismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. Then the defendant preferred Civil Revision No.1400 of 1997 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule which upon hearing the par-ties was made absolute. Being aggrieved heirs of the plaintiffs filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1449 of 2003 before this Division and leave was granted giving rise to the instant appeal.
5. Mr. Zainul Abedin, learned Advocate-on-Record on behalf of the appellants-plaintiffs submitted that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in failing to consider that both the Courts below after considering the entire evidence on record concurrently found that the plaintiffs suit is maintainable but the High Court Division without adverting those findings abruptly held that the suit is barred by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. He further submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in failing to consider that both the Courts below disbelieved the defendant's claim regarding title and possession over the suit land, and those concurrent findings being finding of fact based on material on record are binding upon the High Court Division an& unless those findings are reversed with proper reasoning the High Court Division cannot reverse those findings and believe the defendant's case whimsically. He lastly submitted that the High Court Division erred in Law in failing to consider that both the Courts below found that the plaintiffs were in possession and subsequently they were dispossessed by defendant No.l. Those concurrent findings being findings of fact are binding upon the High Court Division unless those findings are reversed with proper reasoning.
6. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1(a)-1(e) made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He submitted that both the Courts below misread, and misunderstood the misconstrued materials on record and consequently failed to comprehend the facts of the case and misapplied the law and came to a wrong decision occasioning miscarriage of justice. He submitted that as a matter of course, the vendors of the plaintiffs had no right to transfer the land In excess of .09 acre according to Exhibit-2 rather the plaintiffs could not furnish any document/instrument or any specific particular in support of their claim. He also submitted Exhibit- 1 demonstrated that Sayed (son of Sarabdi) and Jashim Molla (son of Dabaru Molla) sold .09 acre land out of the suit plot to one Nuki Molla by a kabala dated 12.02.1942 A.D. and further Entaj Ali Molla and Kubbat Ali Molla, sons of Mohan Molla transferred .09 acre of land out of the suit plot to the said Nuki Molla by a kabala dated 08.03.1948 A.D. (vide Exhibit-3) despite, the plaintiffs did not express anything with regard to this prospect in the plaint which appears to be the non-disclosure of material facts. He further stated that the plaintiffs submitted a kabala (Exhibit-5) with a view to show that they had purchased .14 acre of land out of the suit plot from one Most. Habijan Bibi and another from Mohammad Ali on 24.01.1963 but in the plaint, no disclosure was made with regard to any such purchase inasmuch there was no evidence to show with regard to the said two vendors had interest in .14 acre of land to sell the same to the plaintiffs as well as the said exhibit was utterly isolated with the plaint in question. Next, he submitted that the plaintiffs claimed .27½ acre of land out of the suit plot by purchase from Fayezuddin and his 5 other brothers (vide Exhibit-4, a kabala dated 20.11.197) but those six brothers had no saleable interest exceeding .09 acre of land to transfer to the plain-tiffs. Since there having been various co-sharers in the suit property the suit for declaration of title with recovery of possession was not maintainable without prayer for a further relief of partition of the suit property. Hence, the suit was not framed properly and was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and as such the High Court Division has rightly decided in passing the impugned judgment which is liable Lo be affirmed and the appeal be dismissed.
7. On perusal of the materials on record it appears that the suit filed by the plaintiffs is for declaration of title and recovery of khan possession of .27½ acre of land forming the western part .55 acre of land appertaining to C.S. I of No.237 of C.S. Ithatian No.32 of Mouza-Char Roy locally known as Rayerchar of Police Station and District-Jamalpur.
8. The plaintiffs claim that the suit property originally belonged to one Adu Molla and after his death it devolved upon his heirs namely Sarabdi Molla, Dabaru Mona and others. They further claim that suit plot No.237 was in the saham of the aforesaid Sarabdi Molla and Dabaru Mona. Sarabdi Molla died leaving behind three sons namely Gahar. Mona, Mahar Molla and Sayed Molla and one daughter but she died without any issue. Dabaru Molla died leaving behind one son namely Jasimuddin and two daughters. Gahar Molla son of late Sarabdi Molla died leaving behind two sons namely Haseri Ali Molla and Kazim Mona and two daughters namely Kulsom Bewa and Batashi Bibi. Hansen Ali Molla purchased the land of the suit plot along with other lands from the heirs of other co-sharers namely Jasimuddin, Sayed and Mohar. Being in possession of the same Hasen Ali Molla his brother Kazirn and two sisters transferred their entire share to Foizuddin and five others who later sold the same to the plaintiffs by registered kabala dated 20.11.1957. After such purchase the plain-tiffs gave the same in barga to defendant No.l. Defendant No.1 delivered barga crops of the suit land to the plaintiffs for 4 to 5 years without any interruption and thereafter in the month of Kartick 1368 B.S. the plaintiffs terminated the barga cultivation and grew pulse in the suit land of their own and when it grew high defendant No.1 along with his kith and kin dis-possessed them from the suit land by removing the pulse on 14.11.1961.
9. On the other hand, admitting the suit property to be the property of Amud Molla defendant No.1 stated in his written statement that it was wrongly recorded in the names of Sarabdi Molla and Dabaru Molla in ejmali and they never possessed the land. The defendant claims that Amud Molla sold the suit land to Bakhar Molla father of defendant No.1 on 21.07.1920 by registered kabala in which Gahar Mona son of Sarabdi Molla was a attesting wit-ness and during operation of the rent-roll survey the plaintiffs unsuccessfully raised objection under section 19A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed.
10. After perusing the materials on record it appears that leave was granted to deter-mine as to (I) whether the suit is barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877; (ii) whether the High Court Division erred in law in failing to consider that both the courts below disbelieved the defendant's claim regarding title and possession over the suit land by giving concurrent findings and the same being finding of fact based on materials on record are binding upon the High Court Division and lastly, OH) whether the High Court Division erred in law in failing to consider that both the courts below found that the plaintiffs were in possession and subsequently they were dispossessed by defendant No.1 and those being concurrent findings of facts are binding upon the High Court Division.
11. The points involved in this appeal as stated above have already been dealt with in accordance with law by the High Court Division while passing the impugned judgment and order.
12. The High Court Division found that the suit land appertaining to C.S. Plot No.237 containing .55 acre of land as set forth in the plaint was recorded in the names of Dabaru Molla and Sarabdt Molla in the remark column of C.S. Khatian No.32 to be in their possession in 8 annas share each. After the death of Sarabdi Mona it devolved upon his sons namely Gahar Molla, Mohor Molla and Sayed Molla and a daughter who died issueless and as such the aforesaid three sons must have inherited .09 acre of land each. After the death of Gahar Molia his sons namely Hasen Molla, Kazim Molla and two daughters namely Kulsom Bewa and Batashi Bibi inherited .09 acre of land jointly left by their Father. Gahar Molla in the suit land. Exhibit-2 shows that the said Kasen Mona, Kazim Molla and their two sisters transferred their shares to the extent of .09 acre of 1 rind to 6(six) brothers namely, Fayezuddin, Ayezuddin, Tayezuddin, Bahezuddin, Hazrat Ali and Hatem Ali by a kabala dated 02.02.1953 A.D. Thereafter, the said Fayezuddin and his .five other brothers transferred .27 acre of land out of the suit plot by a kabala dated 20.11.1957 to the plaintiffs vide Exhibit-4. In this respect the High Court Division reached to a definite conclusion that although they had no right to transfer the land in excess of .09 acre of land which was purchased by them through Exhibit-2, but they transferred .27V2 acre of land which is beyond their saleable interest and which is not in accordance with law. The High Court Division also observed that Exhibit-1 shows Sayed son of Sarabdi Molla nad Jasim Molla son of Dabaru Mot la sold .09 acre of land out of the suit plot to one Nuki Molla by a kabala dated 12.02.1942 A.D. and Entaj Ali Molla and Kubbat Ali Molla both sons of Mohar Molla transferred .09 acre of land out of the suit plot to the said Nub Molla by a kabala dated 08.03.1948 A.D. but the plaintiff 8 did not state anything about the same in the plaint which is non disclosure of material facts which are relevant and necessary for proper adjudication of the ease between the parties. By submitting Exhibit-5 although the plaintiffs tried to show that they had purchased .14 acre of land out of the suit plot from one Most. Habljan Bibi and another Mohammad Ali on 24.01.1963 but they did not state anything about any such purchase in the plaint. Moreover, it was rightly held that there was no evidence as to how the said two vendors had interest in .14 acre of land to sell the same to the plaintiffs and as such the said Exhibit-5 is wholly unconnected with their plaint.
13. This being the position of the case, the High Court Division came to a definite finding that there being various co-sharers in the snit property and the plaintiffs having failed to prove their claim in .271/2 acre of land in its entirety and for also that the suit property having been recorded in the names of the plaintiffs, defendants and their predecessors as admitted in the plaint the suit for declaration of title with recovery of possession was not maintainable without prayer for a further relief of partition of the suit property. As such, the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.
14. The same view was taken in the case of Nuruzzaman Sarkar Vs. Sera] Mia and others, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 106 wherein it was held as follows:
"It is a suit for declaration that the Vested Property Case is illegal, collusive and void. Now that the appellant is not found to have title to the entire suit land the greater part of which is in fact an enemy and vested property, the appellant-plaintiff is not entitled to a decree he prayed for. He may seek remedy by way of partition in an appropriate forum"
15. In the case of Enjaheruddin Mia Vs. Mohammad Bossain and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 84 it was held as follows:
"I he proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act (Act I of 1877) provides that no court shall make any declaration as to the plaintiffs' legal character or his right to any property where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title omits to do so. So far as the instant case is concerned the plaintiffs could have asked for either joint possession or partition as a co-sharer of the defendants in the disputed land but they did not take any such stand in the lower appellate Court or even before the High Court Division.
In such view of the matter it will not at all be fair to put blame either upon the lower appellate Court or the High Court Division that they did not declare plaintiffs' title to the part or the suit land.
In the facts and circumstance of the case the lower appellate Court appears to have lightly held that the suit for mere declaration as framed is not maintainable."
16. In respect of possession of the defendants in the suit land, the High Court Division upon going through the testimony of P.W.1 found that there was no barga kabuliyat in respect of the barga settlement to defendant No. 1. Nobody was also present at the time of talking about the said barga settlement. Hasen Ali Molla who as per his statement knew about delivery of barga crops by defendant No.1 to the plaintiffs was not examined as witness.

<u>17. Accordingly, the High Court Division observed that the defendants inherited the suit land from their father Bakhar Molla who had purchased the same from Amud Molla (father of Sarabdi Molla and Dabaru Molla) vide kabala dated 21.07.1920 A.D. In which Gahar Molla son of Sarabdi Molla was an attesting wit-ness. In respect of recording of quantum of land of .63 acre in the kabala instead of .55 acre, the High Court Division observed that the defendants could not show any document that C.S. Plot No.237 contained an area of .63 acre of land and that at any stage of C.S. operation it was recorded in the name of Amud Molla. But, however defective the said kabala might appear, contesting defendant's possession in the suit land on the basis of the said kabala above the statutory period of limiation could not be brushed aside. Moreover, the defendants names were also admittedly recorded in the S.A. Khatian in respect of the suit property and the plaintiffs' objection under section 19A of the SAT Act, 1950 was rejected finding it to be in the possession of the defendants. Rather it is well settled principle of law that the plaintiff had to prove his case in order to get the decree prayed for, in no way the burden can be shifted over the defendants to do so.</u>
18. The aforesaid finding and decision arrived at by the High Court Division being based on proper appreciation of fact and law the same does not call for any interference by this Division.
19. Accordingly, this civil appeal is dis-missed without however, any order as to costs.
End.

full_judgment:
In this Civil Revision, the Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 27-7-2015 (decree signed on 2-8-2015) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Netrokona in Other Appeal No.46 of 2015, allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 27-1-2015 (decree signed on 2-2-2015) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Netrokona in Other Class Suit No.128 of 2001, decreeing the suit shall not be set-aside and/or why such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper, shall not be passed.
2. Pending hearing of the Rule, the parties were directed to maintain status quo in respect of possession and position of the suit property.
3. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No.128 of 2001 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Netrokona praying for a decree of permanent injunction against the defendants. The plaintiffs' case in short, is that the suit land measuring 0.30 acre appertaining to CS Khatian No.46, SA Khatian No.40, SA Plot No.27, Mouza-Gondorpur, Police Station and District- Netrokona belonged to Md Dulal Mia and Abul Hossain. The plaintiff vide registered kabala No.131 dated 25-4-1989 purchased 0.20 acre of land from Md Dulal Mia and Abul Hossain by registered kabala No.648 dated 18-1-2001 and also purchased 0.10 acre of land from Abut Hossain vide registered kabala No.648 dated 18-1-2001. Accordingly, delivery of possession was made and the plaintiff has been possessing the same by making homestead, pond and planting trees. Earlier in a suit for partition bearing No.203 of 1990, the plaintiff and his vendor got a sole decree regarding 0.47 acre of land including the suit land. The defendants have no title and possession in the suit land but on 14-7-2001, the defendants forcibly tried to take over possession of the suit property. Accordingly, the plaintiff filed the instant suit.
4. Defendant Nos.1-4 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. Their specific case is that one Jamini Sundari purchased 1.91 acres of land on auction in Tax Execution Case No.43 of 1937, arisen out of Tax Suit No.1328 of 1936. Maleka Khatun, wife of Abul Hossain who is the maternal father-in-law of the plaintiff purchased 10 decimals of land appertaining to plot No.40 vide registered kabala No.974 dated 1-2-2000. Farida Yeasmin, maternal mother-in-law of the plaintiff also purchased 10 decimals of land from plot No.40 from Manmohan Chandra Barman and Jatindra Chandra Barman who were the grandsons of Jamini Sundari. Defendant No.2, Tara Mia who is also a maternal grandfather of the plaintiff purchased 10 decimals of land from plot No.40 vide registered kabala No.1985 dated 13-4-1997 from Manmohan Chandra Barman and Jatindra Chandra Barman who were also the grandson of Jamini Sundari. Accordingly, he mutated his name vide 'Mutation Miscellaneous Case No. 308(9)/ 1997-1998. While, Tara Mia was in possession and enjoyment of the said property, he sold the same by registered kabala No.1828 dated 6-4-1998 to one Md Nurul Islam. Defendant No.2, Tara Mia and the said Nurul Islam sold 11.5 decimals of land from plot No.40 to Chitta Ranjan Paul, husband of defendant No.4, Ratna Paul vide registered kabala No.6680 dated 7-10-1999. Defendant No.4 again purchased 0.50 decimals of land from plot No.40 from one Samir Datta (Swapan) vide registered kabala No.6937. Defendant No.4 further purchased 10 decimals of land from suit plot No.27 from said Manmohan Chandra Barman and Jatindra Chandra Barman vide registered kabala No.6949 dated 18-10-1999. Thus, Ratna Paul became the owner of 12 decimals of land in plot No.40 and 10 decimals of land in plot No.27 i.e. in total 22 decimals of land. Ratna Paul is possessing and enjoying the same properties through his brother-in-law Dhananjoy Paul, defendant No.1 by making house, homestead and pond. Defendant No.3 also purchased 1 decimals of land from plot No.27 vide registered kabala No.4255 dated 19-7-2001 from Jatindra Chandra Barman for making a path way. Thus, the plaintiff has no right and title in the suit property and accordingly, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.
5. During trial the plaintiffs examined 5(five) witnesses and exhibited some documents which were marked as Exhibits 1 to 7. On the other hand, the defendants also examined 3(three) witnesses and also exhibited some documents which were marked as Exhibits 'Ka' series to `Ta'.
6. Upon hearing both the parties, the Trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 27-1-2005 (decree signed on 2-2-2005) decreed the suit.
7. Against the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, the defendant-opposite parties preferred Other Appeal No.46 of 2005 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Netrokona and the appeal was transferred to the Court of Additional District Judge, Netrokona for its disposal. Upon hearing both the parties, the Court of Appeal below by the judgment and decree dated 27-7-2015 (decree signed on 2-8-2015) allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit and thereby reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court.
8. Against the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below, the plaintiff filed the instant Civil Revision and obtained the Rule and the order of status quo.
9. Having placed the Civil Revisional Application, Mr Khalequzzaman Masud, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the Court of Appeal below reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court without reversing the material finding on the prima facie title and exclusive possession of the plaintiff in the suit property and thereupon committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.
10. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that in support of his possession, the petitioner also submitted the rent receipts and tax receipts issued by the local union parishad but, the Court of Appeal below without considering even this documentary evidence on possession came to the erroneous finding resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.
11. The learned Advocate for the petitioner lastly submits that since the plaintiff got a sole decree in Partition Suit No.203 of 1998, the title of the plaintiff was established therein and in the present suit, he has also been successful to prove his exclusive possession in the suit property and, as such, the Court of Appeal below without considering the said judgment and decree passed in the said Partition Suit erroneously held that the title of the plaintiff could not be ascertained in such a suit while, he also failed to consider the plaintiff's exclusive possession in the suit property and thus, the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below being not a proper judgment and decree of reversal, the same is liable to be set-aside and accordingly, the Rule should be made absolute.
12. On the other hand, Mr Shishir Kanti Mazumder, learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite parties submits that it appears from the case of both the parties that there are claim and counter claim over the suit property by certain registered kabala and both the parties also adduced and produced evidence in support of their respective possession. Therefore, the Court of Appeal below rightly held that the proportionate title and possession cannot be ascertained in a suit for permanent injunction simplicitor and thus, the suit is not maintainable.
13. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties then submits that the Trial Court did not take into consideration of the registered deeds and registered bia deeds of the defendants though those were exhibited and thereupon came to an erroneous decision while, the Court of Appeal below having appreciated all the material evidence on record came to the right decision and accordingly, there being no legal infirmity in the impugned judgment and decree, the Rule is liable to be discharged.
14. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties further submits that the plaint does not disclose the source of title of the vendor of the plaintiff while, Jamini Sundari purchased the suit property along with some other properties on auction in Tax Execution Case No.43 of 1937, arisen out of Tax Suit No.1328 of 1936 and accordingly, produced and exhibited certified copy of the writ of delivery of possession and the defendants are the successive purchaser either from the grandson of Jamini Sundari or from the vendor who purchased the same from the heirs of Jamini Sundari and accordingly, they have been in exclusive possession and accordingly, the Court of Appeal below justly and fairly dismissed the suit upon allowing the appeal.
15. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties again submits that the plaintiffs case does not disclose that the defendants were parties in Partition Suit No.203 of 1990 while, in the present suit, the plaintiff could not disprove the auction sale, the bia deed and purchased deed and thus, the Court of Appeal below came to the right decision in allowing the appeal and dismissing the suit.
16. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties also submits that the plaintiff failed to prove the cause of action by adducing and producing any reliable witness and thus, there being no cause of action in the suit for permanent injunction, the Court of Appeal below rightly dismissed the same upon allowing the appeal.
17. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties lastly submits that even as per the case of both the parties, both the parties are in joint possession of the suit property, permanent injunction cannot be granted against the defendants without asserting their title in a proper suit and, as such, there is no legal infirmity in the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below occasioning failure of justice and thus, the Rule is liable to be discharged.
18. I have perused the Civil Revision Application along with the records of the Courts below and heard the learned Advocates from both sides.
19. As per the plaintiff's case, he purchased 20 decimals of land appertaining to.SA Plot No.27 vide registered kabala No.131 dated 25-4-1989 from Md Dulal Mia and Abul Hossain and then he also purchased 10 decimals of land from the same plot vide registered kabala No.648 dated 18-1-2001 from Abul Hossain and he has been in possession of the same by making house, homestead, pond and planting trees and residing herein with his family. The plaintiff's further case is that regarding 47 decimals of land including the suit land, Partition Suit No.203 of 1990 was decreed on compromise between the plaintiff and Abul Hossain. On the other hand, as per the defendants' case, they or their vendor did not purchase any property from Abul Hossain rather, it appears that Maleka Khatun, wife of Abul Hossain purchased 10 decimals of land from the heirs of auction purchaser Jamini Sundari and Farida Yeasmin also purchased 10 decimals of land from the heirs of Jamini Sundari. Defendant No.4 also purchased 10 decimals of land from the heirs of Jamini Sundari. Subsequently, defendant No.2 sold his property to Nurul Islam. Then Chitta Ranjan Paul, husband of defendant No.4 purchased 11.5 decimals of land from Nurul Islam and defendant No.2. Subsequently, Ratna Paul again purchased 0.50 decimals of land by the registered deed as has been mentioned above. Then Ratna Paul also purchased 10 decimals of land appertaining to suit plot No.27 from the heirs of Jamini Sundari. Even, as per the case of the plaintiff, he purchased 47 decimals of land in plot No.27 while, the defendant No.4 purchased 10 decimals of land out of that 47 decimals of land and it is the case of the defendants that defendant No.4 has been possessing and enjoying her purchased property measuring 22 decimals of land which forms a compact piece of land appertaining to plot Nos.40 and 27.
<u>20. It also appears that both the parties adduced and produced evidence in support of their respective possession. The plaintiff claimed that he has been in possession of the suit land by making homestead, pond and planting trees. On the other hand, it is also the specific case of the defendants that the defendant No.4 has been possessing her property through her brother-in-law, defendant No.1 by making houses, homestead, pond and planting trees. Since in the suit property, both the parties claimed that their residential houses situate thereon, it cannot be said that either of the parties has no possession in the suit property rather, it appears that both the parties are in possession of the suit property and they have also produced documents in support of their respective title as well as rent receipts in support of their possession. Accordingly, without deciding their right, title and possession in the suit property in a suit for partition, the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree for permanent injunction against the co-sharer. Therefore, the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner.</u>
21. Thus, I do not find any legal infirmity in the findings and observations of the Court of Appeal below which occasioned failure of justice. Accordingly, I do not find any merit in the Rule.
22. Hence, the Rule is discharged.
However, there would be no order as to costs.
Send down the lower Courts' records immediately.
End.

full_judgment:
ASM Abdul Mobin, J: In this Rule the petitioners have challenged the judgment and decree dated 9-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Bandarban in Civil Appeal No. 25 of 2016 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 16-7-2016 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Bandarban in Other Suit No. 106 of 2015 dismissed the suit.
2. The opposite parties being plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 184 of 2010 in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, Bandarban. Suit was transferred to the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Bandarban and the suit was renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 106 of 2015. In the plaint the plaintiff stated inter alia that land measuring 2.56 acre in the holding Nos. 52, 34, 154 appertaining to Khatian No. 46 under 288 Alikadam Mouza of AliKadam Police Station, Bandarban Hill District was recorded in the name of Krasing Tonchaingya. Subsequently, Krasing Tonchaingya sold out of 1.53 acre of land out of 2.56 to Liakat Ali, Zinnath Ali, Saber Miah, Abdur Rahim, Ramath Ali and Md Zalcaria and the land was recorded in their names through Mutation Case No. Ak 35/1995. They have been owning and possessing the land since their purchase. While they were possessing the land, .the defendant dispossessed them on 15-8-2010 in their absence from 0.10 decimal of land in plot No. 1284 out of 1.50 acre of their purchased land. The defendant had no right title and interest in the suit land. The defendant No.1 claimed to have purchased 0.10 decimals of land appertaining to the same khatian from plaintiff No.4. An application was filed before the Deputy Commissioner Bandarban and an enquiry was held. In the inquiry report it is alleged that the defendant No.6 was possessing a piece of land measuring 513 feet within ten decimals land appertaining to the same khatian. Earlier defendant Nos. 1-2 and two others dispossessed the plaintiff from a portion of their land in the year of 2008 and when they were dispossessed, one co-sharer of the plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 24 of 2008. After filing of the suit the land was released and made over the possession to the plaintiffs. It is further alleged in the plaint that cause of action was arisen on 15-7-2010. Since the plaintiffs were dispossessed illegally, they filed the instant suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, for recovery of their khas possession.
3. In the suit the defendants filed separate written statements defendant Nos. 1, 2-5, 8-10, 11 and 12 filed separate written statements. The defendant No.1 in his written statement stated inter alia that the land measuring four acres in the holding number R-185 under 288 Alikadam Mouja, Bandarban Hill District was recorded in the name of the Government and Abdul Gafur Miah father of the defendant No.1 was shown to have been possessor the land. The defendant No.1 took settlement of the land through settlement case No. 7208/1980-81. He sold out 28 decimal land to one Mohsin Ali Thereafter, he sold out 40 decimals of land to defendant Nos. 2-5 by registered deed. The defendant Nos.2-5 have been owning and possessing the land after their purchase. After the aforesaid sales the defendant No.1 possessing 3.39 acre land. The defendant categorically stated that they had not dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. The land allegedly purchased from Krasing Tonchaingya was not demarcated. On the other hand, the land of the defendants were wall demarcated.
4. The defendant Nos. 2-5 in their written statement stating the same fact. They further stated that they had purchased the land from defendant No.1. They have been owning and possessing the same since their purchase.
5. Defendant Nos. 8, 10 and 11 in their written statements stated that they rented the shop premises from the defendants and they had been running business in their shop premises. Defendant No. 12 a government official stated that the defendant No.1 took settlement from the government.
6. The suit was tried. In the trial 3 PWs were examined in favour of the plaintiff on the other hand 4 DWs were examined on behalf of the defendants. Both the parties adduce documentary evidence in their evidence. The learned Senior Assistant Judge on consideration of evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit on the ground that in the plaint the plaintiffs alleged to have been dispossessed from the suit land on 5-8-2010. But in the later part of the plaint it is stated that the cause of action of the suit was arisen on 15-7-2010. Moreover, it is further stated that the defendant No.6 dispossessed the plaintiff on 15-7-2010. Earlier another suit being Other Class Suit No. 24 of 2008 was filed. As the defendant released the land and made over the possession to them, the suit was not prosecuted and accordingly it was dismissed. On the above findings learned Senior Assistant Judge dismissed the suit.
7. The plaintiff being aggrieved filed Civil appeal No. 25 of 2016 in the Court of District Judge, Bandarban. The learned District Judge allowed the appeal holding that the PW 1 the attorney of the defendants in his evidence claimed to have dispossessed by the defendants on 5-8-2010. Defendant did not claim the suit land. Their claim was in respect of the land under holding No. 185 which was different land and their land was hundred feet away from the suit land. Therefore, the facts of dispossession was proved and accordingly the learned District Judge allowed the appeal and decreed the suit. Thereafter, the defendant moved this Court and obtained the Rule.
8. Mr Mohiuddin, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner on his submission raises the question of maintainability of the appeal in the Court below. He submits that section 9 of the Specific Relief Act categorically provides that no appeal shall lie against the judgment and decree passed by under this section. He, accordingly, submits that the very appeal in the Court below is without jurisdiction and, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the Court of below is also liable to be set-aside. In support of his contention, he refers to the case of Nawalnada Mahammad Umar Khan vs Muhammad Asif and others 16 DLR (WP) 164, Kanai Lal Ghose vs Jatindra Nath Chandra XXII CWN 446 and ASM Mahbub Elahi vs Md Shah Alam and others BCR 2004 HCD 157 = 8 BLC 484.
9. Mr Motiur Rahman, learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party on the other hand submits that the very appeal filed in the Court below is very much maintainable. He refers to the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation 1900. In the Regulation No. 8(5) of the Regulation specifically provides for filing an appeal before the learned District Judge against the judgment and decree passed by the Joint District Judge. In view of the said provision of law the very appeal is very much maintainable. The leaned advocate also refers to the fact that the appellate Court on clear finding that the plaintiffs opposite parties were dispossessed illegally by the defendants and before dispossession they were in possession. They right title and possessions were also established. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned District Judge rightly passed the judgment and decree.
10. I have considered the submissions of the learned advocates appearing for both the sides. In this revision the learned advocate for the defendant-petitioners raises a preliminary question of jurisdiction as to whether the appeal in the Court District Judge is maintainable or not. Admittedly the suit was filed under section 9 of the Specific Reliefs Act, 1877. Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, is as follows:—
"If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.
Nothing in this section shall bar any person suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.
No suit under this section shall be brought against the Government.
No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed."
<u>11. This section is a special provision for providing quick remedy to a person who has been dispossessed from his immovable property otherwise in due course of law. In the suit plaintiff is not required to establish his title. He can succeed only showing his previous possession and wrongful dispossession. The proceedings under the section do not constitute a bar against either of the parties suing to establish his title to the property and to recover possession thereof. Thus the party adversely affected in a suit under section 9 of Specific Relief Act have alternative remedy by way of regular suit for establishing title and recovering possession.</u>
12. The learned advocate for the plaintiff opposite party on the other hand refers to the provision of Regulation No. 8 of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation 1900. Regulation No. 8(5) of the Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900 provides for filing appeal against judgment and decree passed by the joint District Judge to the District Judge. In the instant case, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Bandarban passed the judgment and decree against which there is no provision to file appeal in the Regulation, 1900. Further section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is a special provision of law where Hill Tracts Regulation is a general law. A special shall always prevail over the general law.
13. In view of the matter 8(5) of the Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900 is no way applicable in the instant case.
14. In the case of Nawabzada Mahammad Umar Khan vs Muhammad Asif and others 16 DLR (WP) 164 it was held:
"It will be seem that the last part of section 9 expressly prohibits an appeal from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section. The power of review is also similarly taken away in respect of any such order or decree."
15. The case of Kanai Lal Ghose vs Jatindra Nath Chandra 22 CWN 446, suit was filed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. Suit was decreed but in the concluding portion of the judgment of the trial Court ran as if the suit was decree against all the defendants though the suit was framed only against defendant No.6 who had resisted the claim. The plaintiff decree holder applied for execution and for recovery of cost from all the defendants. The trial Court held that the decree was in essence against the contesting defendant alone and dismissed the application for execution of the decree against other defendants.
16. The plaintiff decree holder appealed before the District Judge. The learned District Judge accepted the contention of the plaintiff decree holder and accordingly directed to proceed against all the defendants. Thereafter, some of the defendant applied for review and contended that the District Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. The learned District Judge accepted contention and discharged his earlier order. Thereafter, the plaintiff went before the High Court and initially the Rule was issued but after hearing High Court discharged the Rule. In that case it was held:
"The position thus is that the appeal was heard by the District Judge without jurisdiction and the review was granted by him equally without jurisdiction, and both these orders must consequently be discharged.’’
17. In the case of ASM Mahbub Elahi vs Md Shah Alam and others BCR 2004 HCD 757 = 8 BLC 484 it was observed:
"When a decree has been passed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in favour of the petitioner, it is binding upon the opposite party No.1 unless it is set-aside/ varied by an order passed under revisional jurisdiction and any order passed by the Court of appeal will be without jurisdiction and not sustainable in law. "
18. In view of the observations of the High Court and discussion made above the very acceptance of the appeal by the Court of below is without jurisdiction and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set-aside.
19. As the appeal was found not maintain-able, it is not at all necessary to enter into discussion on merit of the case.
20. In view of the matter, I find substance in this Rule.
21. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute and the judgment and decree dated 9-11-2020 passed in Civil Appeal No. 25 of 2016 passed by the learned District Judge, Bandarban is hereby set-aside.
22. The order stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby recalled and vacate.
Send down the LCR along with a copy of this judgment to the Courts below at once
End.
