full_judgment:
Md Akhtaruzzaman, J: This miscellaneous appeal under section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure (shortly, the Code) is directed against the judgment and order dated 29-4-2015 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Nilphamari in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 2011 filed under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 allowing the pre-emption.
2. Facts relevant for disposal of the instant appeal, in short, are that respondent No. 1 as pre-emptor filed the above-mentioned case before the learned Joint District Judge, Nilphamari contending, inter alia, that the impugned land along with other lands was vested and non-resident property of the government and SA Khatian Nos. 2328 and 2325 were prepared accordingly. 1. (one) decimal land of plot No. 8292 and 11 (eleven) decimals of plot No. 8289 were handed over to Hasina Begum, wife of Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda, who subsequently got mutated her name in the said land vide Mutation proceeding No. 302/1995-1996. After the demise of her first husband Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda, Hasina Banu got married to the present petitioner. Later on, Hasina Banu died leaving behind the petitioner as her husband and opposite party No. 2 Mirza Shamsul Wara Nazmul Huda and opposite party No. 4 Mst. Habiba Shams Mukta as her heirs. The petitioner is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case land whereas the opposite party No. 1 is an stranger-purchaser. Opposite party No. 2 on 3- 1-2011 without serving any notice sold out the case land vide Kabala Deed No. 34 in favour of opposite party No. 1. The petitioner came to know about the transfer on 5-1-2011 and upon getting certified copy of the same on 6-1-2011 filed the instant case upon observing the legal formalities.
3. The case was contested by opposite party No. 1. In the written objection, opposite party No. 1 states that the case is barred by the principle of estoppels, waiver, and acquiescence; the case is bad for defect of parties; the petitioner is not a co-sharer in the case land. It is further stated that Hasina Banu got married to Captain Shamsul Huda before 1971 and during the marriage, she gave birth to a son, Md Sharnsul Wara Nazmul Huda and a daughter Mst. Habiba Shams Mukta. Captain Shamsul Huda was killed on 30th March 1971 in Cumilla Cantonment. The case land was given allotment by the government in favour of Hasina Banu, wife of Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda and eventually, it was registered in favour of her on 27-6-1995 vide Kabala Deed No. 4529. Hasina Banu did not get married to the petitioner. After the death of Hasina Banu, opposite party No. 2 transferred the case land on 3-1-2011 to opposite party No. 1. The petitioner knew the matter.
4. In order to prove the respective claims, both the parties adduced evidence. On consideration of the evidence and materials on record, the learned Joint District Judge, Nilphamari vide judgment and order dated 29-4-2015 allowed the case.
5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order, opposite party No. 1 being the appellant preferred this miscellaneous appeal, contending, amongst others, that the trial Court had failed to consider the facts as well as the evidence on record; the petitioner is not a co-sharer by inheritance in the case land; the opposite party No. 1 is not a stranger-purchaser; etc. But the learned Joint District Judge most illegally allowed the case which is liable to be set-aside.
6. No one appears for the appellant.
7. It is to be noted here that the instant appeal has arisen against the judgment and decree passed in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 2011 where respondent No. 1 sought pre-emption for the case land. In the said case main questions that arose before the trial Court as well as before this Division are whether respondent No. 1 is a co-sharer by inheritance in the disputed property and whether he filed the case within the statutory period of limitation. Except for these two legal issues, all are factual issues that might be proved or disproved by the contending parties by adducing oral and documentary pieces of evidence. We have observed that both the parties adduced evidence. Thereafter on consideration of the evidence and materials on record, the trial Court allowed the case. Opposite party No. 1 preferred this appeal in 2015. But the appellant remains absent while the appeal is ready for hearing. The matter was posted in the daily cause list with the names of the concerned Advocate. In spite of that, the learned Advocate did not take any steps for hearing of the appeal.
8. Considering the above circumstances, before entering into merit of the case, we feel it necessary to discuss some of the problems in the disposal of civil appeals where the appellants are deliberately absent or sought so many adjournments keeping in mind that in case of dismissal of appeal for default, the appellant has right to re-admit the same if he so desires. In the situation, the pertinent questions which arose before us are as follows:
(1) Whether, in the absence of an appellant or his counsel, an appellate Court should dismiss the appeal in default or decide the appeal on merit?
(2) Whether under such circumstances the appellate Court has jurisdiction to dispose of the appeal on merit?"
9. Under Rule 16 of Order XLI of the Code an appeal should be heard in the presence of the appellant and Rule 17 provides that where on the day fixed for hearing the appellant does not appear, the Court may pass an order of dismissal of the appeal. The Code does not permit the appellate Court to dispose of an appeal on merit.
10. Rule 17 of Order XLI of the Code runs as follows:
1. Dismissal of appeal for appellant's default: Where on the day fixed, or on any other day to which the hearing may be adjourned, the appellant does not appear when the appeal is called on for hearing, the Court may make an order that the appeal be dismissed.
2. Hearing appeal ex-parte: Where the appellant appears and the respondent does not appear, the appeal shall be heard ex-parte."
11. The dismissal provided for by Rule 17(1) of Order XLI is not a dismissal on merit, but a dismissal only for default of appearance. The sub-rule does not require the Court to give any hearing to the respondent even if he is present or to refer to any part of the proceedings as Rule 30 of Order XLI of the Code does. Further, the only order which it authorized the Court to pass is that the appeal be dismissed and in no circumstance is it possible for the Court to dispose of the appeal in any other manner. If disposal of an appeal on merit is within the scope of Rule 17(1) of Order XLI of the Code it would necessarily have made provision for such disposal and it could not have limited the power of the Court to an order that the appeal be dismissed. It is also significant in this connection that the legislature has not chosen to say that the Court may 'dismiss the appeal' instead of 'make an order that the appeal be dismissed'. These two expressions are not identical in meaning and effect may be gathered from a reference to Rule 11 of Order XLI of the Code. Under Sub-rule (1) of Rule 11 of Order XLI of the Code the Court 'may dismiss the appeal', but, in juxtaposition to it, under sub-rule (2) of the same Rule it is said, the Court may 'make an order that the appeal be dismissed'. This difference in the language used in the two sub-rules of the same Rule cannot but be regarded as suggestive of a difference in the nature and content of the legal acts performed by the Court in the two different situations contemplated by them.
12. The conclusion appears to be obvious that an order that the appeal be dismissed, under Rule 17(1) of Order XLI, has to be based merely on the grounds of absence of the appellant and cannot be based on merit. On this point, there is no disagreement. But when a Court proceeds to consider the merit in the situation mentioned in Rule 17(1) of Order XLI of the Code, whether it is competent to travel outside the provision of the said sub-rule and to decide the appeal on merit.
13. It is widely accepted in the legal arena that under Rule 17(1) of Order XLI of the Code, the appellate Court has no jurisdiction to hear the appeal on merit where the appellant does not appear at the time the appeal is called on for hearing. The only course open to the appellate Court is to make an order of adjournment of the case to another date or to make an order of dismissal of the appeal for default.
14. In the context of the question under discussion, the most important feature of Rule 17(1) of Order XLI is its permissive character. It provides that in the situation mentioned therein the Court 'may' make an order that the appeal be dismissed, and not that the Court 'shall' make such an order. The language used in the sub-rule, while empowering the Court to act in a particular manner, does not cast upon it the obligation to act in that manner alone and in no other, and it leaves the Court free to act in such other manner as may be authorized by or justified in law. It only confers upon the Court A discretion which the Court would not otherwise possess and does not bind the Court to the particular course of action provided under it.
15. The use of the word 'may' or 'shall' is certainly not decisive of the enabling or imperative nature of a statutory provision, and  there may he cases where, having regard to the  nature and object of the act contemplated by a ,statute and to the rights of persons for whose benefit it is to be done, the word 'may' has to be read as imposing a duty as well. But, prima facie, and in the absence of the considerations mentioned above, there is no compulsive force in the word 'may' and it connotes merely a power and a discretion. It is well to bear in mind in this connection the words of Cotton, L. J. in re, Baker; Nichols vs Baker (1890) 44 Ch D 262:
"I think that great misconception is caused by saying that in some cases 'may' means 'must'. It never can mean 'must' so long as the English language retains its meaning, but it gives a power and then it may be a question in what cases, where a Judge has a power given him by the word 'may', it becomes his duty to exercise it."
16. There is nothing in the nature and object of the act empowered by Rule 17(1) of Order XLI nor is there any such right in the person for whose benefit the power has been conferred, to couple the power with the duty to do that act and no other. In fact, there are compelling reasons for holding that the legislature employed the word 'may' with the deliberate object of conferring upon the Court the power to act in the manner indicated in the sub-rule, and yet of leaving it free to act in such other mariner as may be permitted by law.
17. Of course, if there had been nothing in the Code empowering the Court to dispose of the appeal of an appellant who is absent at the hearing in any other manner save the one provided by Rule 17(1) of Order XLI, it would have been indisputable that in case the appeal is not adjourned it has to be dealt with in the manner provided by the said provision. But if there is under the Code a general power of dealing with an appeal otherwise as well, that power, unless expressly excluded, will remain exercisable by the Court even where Rule 17(1) of Order XLI is applicable. In that case, the power conferred by Rule 17(1) of Order XLI has to be regarded only as an additional power that may be used in the situation mentioned in it and not as also a limitation upon the generality of the power given elsewhere.
18. The general power of the Court of Appeal is contained in Rules 30, 32, and 33 of Order XLI of the Code.
19. Rules 32 and 33 of Order XLI are dependent upon Rule 30 of the Order since they postulate the power to give judgment and this power is conferred by Rule 30. Rule 30 of Order XLI of the Code runs thus:
"30. Judgment when and where pronounced.—The appellate Court, after hearing the parties or their pleaders and referring to any part of the proceedings, whether on appeal or in the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, to which reference may be considered necessary, shall pronounce judgment in open Court, either at once or on some future day of which notice shall be given to the parties or their pleaders."
20. If the Court may act under this provision even where the appellant is not present when the appeal is called on for hearing it would be of necessity to follow that the Court is possessed with the jurisdiction to pronounce judgment in the manner laid down in Rules 31, 32 and 33 of Order XLI and, therefore, also to dismiss the appeal on merit. There is, however, one essential condition for the pronouncement of judgment and that is, that the parties or their pleaders have to be heard. The question naturally arises whether this essential condition can be deemed to be satisfied if the appellant and his pleader are absent.
21. In this regard Rule 16 of Order XLI is also relevant which is reproduced below: "16(1). Right to begin.—On the day fixed, or on any other day to which the hearing may be adjourned, the appellant shall be heard in support of the appeal.
2. The Court shall then, if it does not dismiss the appeal at once, hear the respondent against the appeal, and in such case, the appellant shall be entitled to reply."
22. Dealing with this Rule the Supreme Court of India in the case of Sukhpal Singh vs Kalyan Singh reported in 119631 2 SCR 733 has observed:
"It is clear from Sub-rule (1) that it is the duty of the appellate Court to hear the appellant in support of the appeal. This, however, does not mean that the appellate Court cannot decide the appeal if the appellant does not make his submissions to the Court showing that the judgment and decree under appeal are wrong. The appellate Court is not to force the appellant to address it. It can, at best, afford him an opportunity to address it. If the appellant does not avail of that opportunity the appellate Court can decide the appeal. Sub-rule (2) indicates that the appeal can be dismissed without hearing the respondent. The appellate Court will do so if it was not satisfied that the judgment under appeal was wrong."
23. The above observations make it clear that a provision enjoining that the appellant shall be heard is complied with if the appellant has been afforded an opportunity of being heard, and it cannot be said that he has not been heard merely because he has not availed of the opportunity given to him. The force of these observations is in no way lessened by the fact that the appellant in that case was present at the hearing but was not prepared to address the Court because it should make no difference in principle whether the failure to avail of the opportunity consists in the absence of the appellant or in his refusal or inability to address the Court in support of the appeal. The essence of the matter is that the opportunity of being heard has been given but has not been availed of. If the requirement of hearing is to be deemed to be fulfilled by giving the appellant who is present an opportunity to be heard it should be regarded as equally fulfilled even in the case of an appellant who has chosen to be absent despite having been allowed to be heard.
24. The principle laid down by the Supreme Court of India regarding Rule 16 of Order XLI applies with equal force to Rule 30 of Order XLI of the Code as well and it must likewise be held that what Rule 30 of Order XLI requires is not that the parties or their pleaders be actually heard but that they should be given an opportunity of being heard. The requirement of Rule 30 of Order XLI of the Code must, therefore, be considered as having been satisfied if the opportunity so given is not availed of, whether the failure to do so consists in the absence of the parties and their pleaders or in their refusal or inability to address the Court. (emphasis given)
25. From the following passage in the judgment of the Supreme Court of India, it is clear that the requisite condition of hearing the parties laid down in Rule 30 of Order XL1 was regarded as fulfilled by virtue of the fact that the opportunity of being heard had been given:
"It is to be noted that this rule does not make it incumbent on the appellate Court to refer to any part of the proceedings in the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred. The appellate Court can refer, after hearing the parties and their pleaders, to any part of these proceedings to which reference be considered necessary. It is in the discretion of the appellate Court to refer to the proceedings. It is competent to pronounce judgment after hearing what the parties or their pleaders submit it for consideration. It follows, therefore, that if the appellant submits nothing for its consideration, the appellate Court can decide the appeal without any reference to any proceedings of the Court below and, in doing so, it can simply say that the appellants have not urged anything which would tend to show that the judgment and decree under appeal were wrong."
26. This decision of the Supreme Court of India, therefore, takes away the authority of those cases in which it has been held that, Rule 30 of Order XLI of the Code can have no application to cases where the appellant does not appear and gives its sanction to the view that the Court may act under Rule 30 of Order XLI even if the appellant has chosen not to avail of the opportunity of being heard either by his absence or by his refusal or inability to support the appeal. We think that Rule 30 of Order XLI applies even in the case of the absence of the appellant at the hearing, there should be little doubt left, that in the situation mentioned in rule 17(I) of Order XLI, the alternatives before the Court are not exhausted between either making an order for dismissal of the appeal for default of appearance or adjourning the case, and the Court has also the option of considering the appeal on merit and confirming, varying or reversing the decree appealed against as provided by rule 32 of Order XLI.
27. We may now refer to some of the cases dealing directly with the questions under consideration.
28. In Chimman Lal and others vs Syed Zahur Uddin reported in AIR 1938 Al! 548, a Division Bench of Allahabad High Court held:
"When an appeal is heard under Order XLI, rule 11, the Court may either act under Sub-rule (1) or Sub-rule (2). Under Sub-rule (1) the dismissal may be on the merits and this may be after hearing the pleader if he appears, but the words indicate that a dismissal on the merits may also be ordered if the pleader does not appear. Under Sub-rule (2) if the appellant does not appear the Court may dismiss for default. But this does not prevent a dismissal on the merits where there is no appearance under Sub-rule (1). The power of the Appellate Court therefore to take these two courses under Rule 11 is not, in our opinion, taken away when a notice is issued to the respondent and the respondent appears in accordance with that notice."
29. In Smt. Gajrani vs Sink Ram Rati reported in AIR 1965 All 547 Allahabad High Court observed that rule 17 of Order XLI permits the appellate Court to follow the procedure of Rule 30 and dismiss the appeal on merit even though the appellant is absent, provided he has had reasonable notice of the date of hearing. The following passage from the judgment brings out the reason for the decision: "In this case, the appeal could have been dismissed by the lower appellate Court in default under rule 17, or on merits under Rule 30 of Order XLI, or could have been adjourned to another date. The word used in Rule 17 is 'may' and not 'shall', and prima facie the legislature intended only to empower the appellate Court to dismiss an appeal in default and not to make it obligatory upon it to do so. Once the word was 'shall' and the legislature substituted it by 'may' clearly indicating its view that it intended to leave the matter at the discretion of the appellate Court. Had the word been 'shall' the appellate Court would have no option but to dismiss the appeal in default and the only consequence of the amendment made by the legislature was to give it discretion. The legislature apparently did not think that an appeal should be dismissed in default regardless of all circumstances and contemplated that in some circumstances it may be more just to dispose of the appeal on merits under Rule 30 or to adjourn it. It may be that ordinarily or in a majority of cases an appellate Court will exercise the discretion in favour of dismissing the appeal in default, but the question is not how the discretion is exercised ordinarily but whether the appellate Court has discretion in the matter at all or not. What order can be passed by an appellate Court if it does not dismiss the appeal in default is not laid down by the legislature; it may be either adjourning the hearing of the appeal or hearing it on merits under Rule 30. I find no words in Rule 17 or any other Rule, expressly or even impliedly, requiring adjournment and prohibiting decision on merits. Hence a decision on merits is not against any provision and can be resorted to by the appellate Court in its discretion."
30. In the case of Balm Ram vs Bhagwan Din and others reported in AIR 1966 All 1, the Full Bench of Allahabad High Court observed:
"Order XLI, rule 30 no doubt makes the hearing of the parties or their pleaders a condition precedent to the pronouncing of judgment, but this condition has been laid down for the benefit of the parties and in their own interest, and its fulfillment is, by its very nature, dependent upon their volition and co-operation. The parties cannot, therefore, by refusing to avail of the benefit and by withholding their cooperation incapacitate the Court for using that power to the exercise of which the condition has been attached. If the opportunity for the fulfillment of the condition has been allowed, although it has not been availed of, the condition will be deemed to have been complied with and the Court will acquire the competence to exercise the power conferred upon it as if the condition has been fulfilled. If this were not so, the parties would, by their own omission to avail of the opportunity granted to them, be able to create an insurmountable impediment in what the Court has been authorised to do by the statute and render the power given to it totally ineffective and nugatory."
31. The Court further held:
"To them, I may only add this, that the appellate Court, in the absence of the appellant, has not the means of knowing the reason of his absence and it is only very rarely that it can be in a position to be firmly convinced that there is no excuse for the appellant's absence and he is deliberately avoiding the hearing of the appeal. The material on which the Court may form an opinion in that matter against the appellant may be untrue, misleading or insufficient, and the circumstances appearing against him may be inconclusive or capable of being explained by the appellant or of being neutralised by other circumstances which the Court does not know and has not the means of knowing at that time. Also, the appeal may have merits which, on account of the absence of the appellant and his counsel, may not be brought to the notice of the Court or the Court may fail to discover. Having regard, therefore, to the serious consequences, that may follow and to the dangers of error, the Court should not ordinarily dismiss the appeal on merits in the absence of the appellant and his counsel, but should leave it open to the appellant to apply under Order XLI, rule 19 and have the dismissal set-aside by satisfying the Court that there was sufficient reason for his absence. It is, in my view, only in exceptional circumstances that the Court should dismiss the appeal on merits in the absence of the appellant and his counsel. What those exceptional circumstances are cannot be rigidly formulated or exhaustively enumerated, and naturally the question under reference does not require it to be done. ... But, it is only after the Court has made up its mind that it will dispose of the appeal on merits and not dismiss it for default of appearance that it will ordinarily inquire into its merits. At the stage of making up its mind in regard to the discretion to be exercised by it, it cannot anticipate what kind of decision the merits of the case would require. The Court may certainly examine the merits of the case also before making its choice between dismissing the appeal for default of appearance of the appellant and deciding it on merits, but that is not what would be done in actual practice. In the normal course, it will be only after the Court has decided to dispose of the appeal that the merits will be examined and the Court will not be in a position to know till then whether the appeal will be allowed or dismissed. The Court must, therefore, have before it the consideration referred to above when it makes no its mind whether, in the absence of the appellant and his counsel it should dismiss the appeal in default of appearance or decide it on merits. And chose consideration would in my opinion persuade the Court not to decide the appeal on merits but only to dismiss it for default unless as I have said above, there are exceptional circumstances demanding a decision on merits."
32. On consideration of relevant provisions and the cases referred to above our considered view is that even in the absence of the appellant and his counsel, the appellate Court has the jurisdiction to dispose of the appeal on merit, i.e., in any of the modes provided by Rules 32 and 33 of Order XLI. We may here state that the appellant's failure to hear in a particular case may also mean his failure to appear either personally or through a counsel, and the word 'absence' about the appellant has been used by us in the wider sense in case of absence of both the appellant and his counsel.
33. In this appeal, we have also perused the relevant Order Book. It appears that the appeal being ready was posted in the daily cause list for a couple of days with the name of the learned Advocate of the appellant but he did not turn up to press the appeal. Accordingly, on 21-11-2016 the appeal was dismissed for default. Thereafter, on an application for re-admission, this First Miscellaneous Appeal was re-admitted on 12-3-2017 with a cost of Taka 5,000 (five thousand), re-calling the dismissal order dated 21-11-2016. It further appears that the appeal was again dismissed for default on 7-5-2018 which was re-called on 16-7-2016 and the appeal was re-admitted to its original file and number. Since the appellant was absent, this appeal was further dismissed for default on 19-11-2018 and this Court vide Order dated 26-11-2018 re-called the order of dismissal with a condition that the appellant should pay a cost of Taka 10,000 (ten thousand) to the respondent within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the order, failing which the appeal shall stand dismissed. Subsequently, on 28-1-2019 the appellant deposited the cost and the appeal was re-admitted. It is also evident from the record that on 8-11-2020 no one appeared for the appellant to press the appeal, when the matter was taken up for hearing and this Court considering the facts and circumstances dismissed the appeal for default. Mr Hasan Rajib Prodhan with Mr Md Ahsanur Rahman, the learned Advocates for the appellant further moved an application for re-admission of the instant appeal and this Court having found prima fade substance vide order dated 2-1-2023 allowed the application with a cost of Taka 3,000 (three thousand) to be paid within 7 (seven) days from the date of receipt of the order. The appellant deposited the money. The appeal was again re-admitted. From the above, it appears that the instant appeal was dismissed for default on several occasions which was eventually re-admitted many times though under Rule 19A of Order XLI of the Code, no appeal shall be re-admitted more than once. It also transpires from the record that on the prayer of the learned Advocate for respondent No. 1 this appeal was fixed for hearing and on the prayer of the learned. Advocate for the appellant, the hearing of the same was adjourned until 30-8-2023. The matter again appeared in the list for hearing but the conduct of the appellant remained unchanged. On 26-11-2023 we heard the learned Advocate of respondent No. 1 and fixed today for delivery of judgment. But the appellant is again found absent which indicates that the appellant has lost her interest in prosecuting the appeal.
34. This first miscellaneous appeal was filed in 2015 and got ready for hearing on 11-8-2016 and since then the appellant has been found absent for hearing the appeal. This unpredictable conduct as well as behaviour of the appellant has delayed the proceedings for a couple of years causing unbearable pain and hardship to the respondent and putting a stigma on the judicial system of our country.
35. Our judiciary is overburdened with a huge backlog of cases. Hundreds of thousands of civil appeals including miscellaneous appeals are pending before the district Courts and in this Division. A considerable number of these types of appeals are pending even for decades after decades. In some occasions, the appellants are deliberately delaying the hearing of the appeals this way or that way keeping in mind the loopholes of the Code. Due to a lack of appropriate legal mechanisms, the Judges are also reluctant to dispose the civil appeals. In some cases, they are under legal obligation to dismiss those appeals for default which have been eventually re-admitted later on under the provisions of Rule 19A of Order XLI of the Code.
36. Considering the status of huge number of pending appeals before the Courts of this Country, we answered the questions mentioned earlier in the positive. After giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard, if the appellant or his counsel fails to hear the appeal, in that circumstances, the appellate Court has jurisdiction to dispose of the appeal on merit and not dismiss the same for default as a routine work.
37. The present Code was adopted by the Legislature in 1908 when the number of pending cases was not so high. Not a significant number of appeals were pending then. Adequate number of judges were working. They had enough time and scope to scrutinize each and every appeals. In case of dismissal for default, the appeals were re-admitted which did not create any backlog of cases. But at present scenario has been changed. The judiciary has been facing huge backlog of cases. Some of the appellants deliberately had been seeking adjournments without any valid reasons. They know that in case of dismissal of the appeal for default, there is scope for re-admission if they so desire which causes unnecessary delay in the disposal of appeals. In this situation, we felt that there is a dire need for amendment of the relevant rule(s) and/or to add a new rule(s) in the Code or in the relevant procedures for early disposal of the long pending appeals to cope with the reduction of the huge backlog of cases.
38. Section 122 of the Code empowers this Division to make rules regulating its own procedure as well as the procedure of the Civil Courts. Section 122 of the Code is reproduced below:
"122. Power of Supreme Court to make rules: The Supreme Court may, from time to time after previous publication, make rules regulating the procedure of each Division of the Supreme Court and the procedure of Civil Courts subject to its superintendence and may be such rules annul, alter or add to all or any of the rules in the First Schedule."
39. In view of the above facts and circumstances, it is our modest expectation that under section 122 of the Code, appropriate steps should be taken to amend and/or add the relevant rules of procedure so that the appellate Courts can dispose of the civil appeals on merit to clear up the unbearable backlog of cases that our judiciary has been facing for decades after decades.
40. Keeping all these matters in view as well as the conduct of the aspirant appellant of the instant appeal, we have decided to dispose of the same on merit.
41. Mr Fazle Rabby, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor respondent No. 1 submits that he is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case land, and after depositing the deed value along with the statutory compensation, the pre-emptor filed the case within the stipulated time. He next submits that the learned Joint District Judge upon considering the oral as well as documentary evidence has correctly passed the impugned judgment and order which need not be interfered with by this Court.
42. Heard the learned Advocate respondent No. 1, perused the impugned judgment and order along with pieces of evidence and materials on record, and also considered the facts and circumstances of the case minutely.
43. With a view to arrive at a correct decision in the instant appeal, we are now required to advert to and weigh the relevant evidence on record in conjunction with the surrounding facts and circumstances of the case.
44. In his evidence, PW 1 Mirza Shamsul Wazed gives out that he is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case land whereas opposite party No. 1 is a stranger purchaser therein. He further states that before purchasing the case land the opposite party did not serve any notice of transfer to him. Opposite party No. 2 secretly transferred the case land to opposite party No. 1 on 3-1-2011 by dint of the impugned kabala deed. He came to know about the disputed deed on 5-11-2011 and after obtaining the certified copy of the same on 6-11-2011 learnt about the transfer in detail and thereafter, filed the case. In support of his claim, P.W.1 submits the relevant documents which have been marked as Exhibit No. 1 series.
45. He denied that he is not a co-sharer by inheritance and filed the case on false plea.
46. PW 2 Md Shamsul Huq Shah corroborates the evidence of PW 1.
47. In her testimony, OPW 1 Hanifa Khatun unfurls that the pre-emptor is the full brother of Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda. In her deposition, she further states that after the death of Shamsul Huda his wife Hasina Banu obtained the property from the government. In cross-examination, she admits that she had heard about the matter of the marriage of Hasina Banu with the petitioner.
49. These are all the evidence that have been adduced by the parties to prove their respective cases.
50. Admittedly, the disputed property was the vested and non-resident property of the government. It is further admitted that Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda, the husband of Hasina Banu was a martyr who sacrificed his life during the war of independence of Bangladesh in 1971. It is also admitted by the parties that Hasina Banu as wife of Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda got 1 (one) decimal of land from Plot No. 8292 and 11 (eleven) decimals of land from Plot No. 8289 from the government vide registered Deed No. 4529 dated 4-10-1995 (Exhibit No. 1). It is further admitted by the parties that after obtaining 12 (twelve) decimals of land, Hasina Banu mutated her name in the said land and received Mutation Khatian No. 5174 [Exhibit No. 1 (3)].
51. It is the definite case of the pre-emptor-respondent No. 1 that after the demise of Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda, the pre-emptor-respondent No. 3 got married with Hasina Banu on 17-7-1988 vide a registered Kabinnama [Exhibit No. 1 (4)]. The pre-emptee-appellant denied the marriage of Hasina Banu with the pre-emptor simply based on the argument that if Hasina Banu got married on 17-7-1988 with the petitioner how her name was mutated in 1995 showing late Captain Shamsul Huda as her husband. In reply to this contention, the learned Advocate of the pre-emptor-respondent No. 1 submits that admittedly Hasina Banu got the suit property from the government as the widow of Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda and for the convenience of getting mutation, she used the name of her former husband. On perusal of Exhibit No. 1 (deed No. 4529 dated 4-10-1995) and Exhibit No. 1 (3) [the mutation Khatian No. 302/1995-96] it appears to us that in those documents, the name of Shahid Captain Shamsul Huda has been used.

During her marriage with Shahid Captain Shamsul 1-luda Hasina Banu gave birth to 2 (two) children (opposite party Nos. 2 and 4 of the pre-emption petition) which is also admitted by the contending parties.
